questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings indicate clinically significant oxygenation compromise? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oxygen saturation of 88% on room air
Blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg
Respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute
Inability to speak in full sentences
Use of accessory muscles

questions.rationale: The strongest indicators of impaired oxygenation are tachypnoea, low oxygen saturation, increased work of breathing, and difficulty speaking in full sentences. Elevated blood pressure may reflect stress or sympathetic response, but it is not the main cue that defines oxygenation failure in this case. NCLEX reasoning focuses on the signs most directly linked to airway and breathing compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s priority clinical interpretation of this situation?

options.text: The patient is experiencing only fever-related discomfort
The patient is mainly anxious and needs reassurance before intervention
The patient is developing acute hypoxaemia and requires immediate respiratory support
The patient is dehydrated and needs oral fluids first

questions.rationale: The most urgent interpretation is acute hypoxaemia. Anxiety may be present, but the nurse must not mislabel a physiological emergency as an emotional issue. The low oxygen saturation, increased work of breathing, and limited speech indicate real respiratory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which nursing problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for impaired skin integrity
Fear related to hospital admission
Ineffective airway clearance and impaired gas exchange related to respiratory distress

questions.rationale: The immediate life-threatening problem is respiratory compromise. In Fundamentals of Nursing, the nurse must always prioritise ABCs above comfort, teaching, or psychosocial concerns when deterioration is present.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the room to look for the physician before intervening
Ask the patient to rest quietly and recheck in 30 minutes
Document the findings before taking any action
Apply oxygen, assess airway patency, position the patient upright, and stay with him while reassessing

questions.rationale: The correct first response addresses airway and breathing immediately. Oxygen support, positioning, assessment, and staying with the patient are all priority actions. Documentation and escalation are important but follow initial stabilising measures.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate after the first response? Select all that apply.

options.text: Evaluate for cough, secretions, or other contributors to the breathing difficulty
Delay escalation if oxygen improves slightly once
Reassess oxygen saturation and respiratory effort after intervention
Monitor mental status because worsening confusion may indicate worsening hypoxia
Prepare to communicate the change using structured handover such as SBAR

questions.rationale: All of these are appropriate. Reassessment and escalation are key NGN principles. Mental status is important because confusion may signal worsening oxygen deprivation. A slight temporary improvement does not remove the need for continued observation and communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Oxygenation Drop and ABC Prioritisation
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates the nurse’s initial interventions are effective?

options.text: Blood pressure stays mildly elevated
The patient coughs once after oxygen is applied
Oxygen saturation improves to 94%, respiratory rate decreases, and the patient can speak more comfortably
The patient says he is tired and wants to sleep without further assessment

questions.rationale: Improved oxygenation, reduced work of breathing, and better ability to speak indicate meaningful respiratory improvement. NGN evaluation focuses on whether the intervention changed the patient’s condition in a safer direction.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings support the need for early airborne precaution planning? Select all that apply.

options.text: Presence of an immunocompromised patient nearby
Night sweats and weight loss
Fever and fatigue
Frequent coughing in a shared ward space
Persistent cough

questions.rationale: All these cues are important. Tuberculosis should be suspected from the symptom cluster, not just one symptom. Shared space and vulnerable nearby patients increase the urgency of prompt infection control.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Isolation can wait until sputum results are final
Suspected airborne infection requires protective action now, even before final confirmation
Because the patient is cooperative, special precautions are unnecessary
A surgical mask for staff provides the same protection as an N95 respirator in this situation

questions.rationale: Infection control is based on risk recognition, not on delayed certainty. The nurse must protect others when symptoms strongly suggest a transmissible airborne disease.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Deficient knowledge about cough etiquette only
Imbalanced nutrition
Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for transmission of an airborne infectious disease to other patients and staff

questions.rationale: The most urgent issue is containment of transmission risk. In Fundamentals, nurses must consider both the patient and the care environment when prioritising safety.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wait for the provider to enter orders before doing anything
Ask the patient to stay quiet to reduce coughing
Initiate airborne precautions, place the patient appropriately according to policy, and use correct respiratory protection
Continue standard precautions only

questions.rationale: The nurse should begin the correct precaution pathway immediately. Waiting or minimising the situation could expose others to preventable harm.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limit unnecessary patient movement through common areas
Use clear communication and signage to support safe isolation practice
Assume a simple surgical mask always gives equivalent airborne protection for staff
Perform hand hygiene before and after patient contact
Ensure visitors and staff follow policy regarding PPE and room entry

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate infection control actions. Airborne precautions require more than just routine masking. Safe practice includes environmental control, PPE, movement restriction, and communication.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best indicates safe nursing management?

options.text: Nearby high-risk patients are not considered in planning
The patient stays in the shared room until all testing is complete
Staff remain unsure about which PPE to wear
The patient is placed under correct precautions promptly, staff use appropriate protection, and exposure risk to others is reduced

questions.rationale: Effective nursing management reduces transmission risk and supports safe care simultaneously.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Why is this order unsafe as written? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insulin is a high-alert medication
The patient’s memory is uncertain
The insulin type is missing
The purpose of the dose is unclear
Multiple insulin preparations are available

questions.rationale: This order is incomplete and therefore unsafe. Because insulin type, timing, and purpose affect onset and risk, the nurse must not assume what was intended. The patient’s uncertainty adds to the need for clarification.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The nurse may select the most common insulin used on the ward
The order must be clarified before any insulin is administered
The nurse should skip the dose indefinitely without follow-up
The patient should decide which insulin is correct

questions.rationale: High-alert medications require complete and accurate orders. Administering based on routine or assumption could cause severe hypo- or hyperglycaemia.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which safety issue is most urgent?

options.text: Delay in meal service
Family visiting arrangements
Risk for medication error and patient harm due to an incomplete high-alert medication order
Documentation workload

questions.rationale: The central issue is patient safety in medication administration. Time pressure does not justify bypassing verification.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wait until after lunch and ignore the missing details
Give the long-acting insulin because it seems safest
Ask another nurse what is usually given and administer that
Clarify the order with the prescriber before giving insulin

questions.rationale: The nurse must verify the order with the prescriber. Peer opinion and routine practice are not substitutes for a valid, complete order.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which actions support safe insulin administration in this situation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Double-check the dose if policy requires it
Clarify the insulin type and intended purpose
Use two patient identifiers before administration
Check the most recent blood glucose result
Skip documentation because insulin is routine

questions.rationale: These are all core medication safety practices. Documentation is always required and should never be skipped, especially for a high-alert drug.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Insulin Order and Medication Clarification
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best shows safe nursing management?

options.text: The chart remains ambiguous but the patient says he trusts the nurse
The nurse delays all diabetic treatment for the rest of the day
The order is clarified, the correct insulin is given, and the administration is documented accurately
The patient receives insulin quickly before lunch without clarification

questions.rationale: A safe outcome includes clarification, correct administration, and proper documentation. NGN evaluation closes the loop from risk recognition to safe completion of care.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings increase this patient’s immediate fall risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confusion and disorientation
Post-operative weakness
Non-slip footwear not in place
Advanced age
Raised bed and inaccessible call bell

questions.rationale: All of these contribute to immediate fall risk. The patient’s age, weakness, cognitive impairment, and unsafe environment combine to create high injury potential.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient is simply restless and can be redirected later
Delirium, weakness, analgesia effects, and environmental hazards are creating an urgent fall risk
The IV line is the only issue
The patient is intentionally non-compliant

questions.rationale: This is a multifactorial safety problem. The nurse should think broadly rather than blaming the patient or reducing the issue to one cause.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Self-care deficit for bathing
Risk for injury related to confusion, weakness, and unsafe mobility attempt
Social isolation

questions.rationale: Preventing immediate physical harm is the top priority. Fundamentals questions often test the nurse’s ability to act on imminent safety threats first.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Explain hospital policy in detail while she stands
Assist the patient back to a safe position and remain with her while addressing the environment
Leave to obtain a restraint order
Document the near fall before intervening

questions.rationale: The patient must be made safe immediately. Documentation and broader planning follow once the imminent risk has been controlled.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use non-slip footwear and reduce clutter
Increase rounding or close observation
Apply restraints immediately as first-line management
Consider toileting needs, pain, and medication effects
Lower the bed and place the call bell within reach

questions.rationale: These interventions reduce fall risk through environment, reassessment, and supervision. Restraints are not first-line and may worsen agitation or injury risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Post-Operative Fall Risk and Immediate Safety
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing management?

options.text: The bed remains high but the nurse documents the risk
The patient remains safe in bed, hazards are reduced, and close observation is in place
The patient stays confused, so the plan is considered ineffective
The call bell stays inaccessible because the patient is forgetful

questions.rationale: Even if confusion persists, the nursing plan is effective when injury risk is reduced and supervision is improved.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings support concern for acute post-operative deterioration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dizziness and weakness
Tachycardia
Pallor and clammy skin
Increased wound drainage
Significant drop in blood pressure

questions.rationale: All of these findings are clinically significant and suggest circulatory compromise. NGN reasoning requires the nurse to integrate the trend rather than viewing the symptoms separately.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of the situation?

options.text: The patient is anxious after surgery and can wait for routine review
The dressing drainage is unimportant if pain is controlled
The blood pressure probably reflects normal variation
The patient may be developing post-operative hypovolaemia or bleeding and requires prompt escalation

questions.rationale: The combination of hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, and increased drainage suggests significant physiological deterioration. Waiting is unsafe.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Acute pain only
Deficient knowledge about wound care
Risk for decreased tissue perfusion related to possible blood loss or shock
Anxiety about surgery

questions.rationale: The patient’s circulation and perfusion are threatened. ABC priorities require the nurse to address this before teaching or reassurance alone.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reassess the patient, ensure immediate safety, and escalate promptly using SBAR or structured communication
Ask the patient to drink water and rest
Finish all routine charting before reporting
Wait until the next observation round

questions.rationale: The nurse should respond immediately with reassessment and escalation. Documentation is important but must not delay urgent communication.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which information should be included in the SBAR handover? Select all that apply.

options.text: Actions already taken by the nurse
The patient’s symptoms such as dizziness and weakness
The vital sign changes and time trend
Relevant surgical background and increased dressing drainage
Objective concern about possible bleeding or hypovolaemia

questions.rationale: A safe handover includes the situation, key background, assessment findings, and response already initiated. This allows the next clinician to act quickly and effectively.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective communication and management?

options.text: The deterioration is recognised early, escalation occurs promptly, and treatment begins while the patient is closely monitored
The change is mentioned later during routine rounds only
The patient remains hypotensive while documentation is prioritised over review
The nurse reports casually without objective findings

questions.rationale: Effective communication improves patient outcomes by enabling timely intervention and coordinated care.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible wound infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increased incisional pain
Mild swelling
Change from previous wound appearance
Fever and chills
Redness and warmth

questions.rationale: All listed findings are consistent with evolving wound infection. The fact that these findings are new or worse than before is especially significant.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient may be developing a surgical site infection requiring prompt assessment and provider notification
Fever is unrelated to the wound
These findings are expected and should be ignored
The wound is healing normally because there is some redness

questions.rationale: The symptom pattern and local wound findings suggest infection until proven otherwise. Dismissing early infection signs may delay treatment and worsen outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for progression of infection related to wound contamination or impaired healing
Knowledge deficit about nutrition
Disturbed sleep pattern
Self-care deficit for grooming

questions.rationale: The nurse must act to prevent a local infection from progressing to systemic illness or impaired wound healing.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the dressing and leave the wound open without assessment
Tell the patient not to worry because redness is normal
Delay review until the next dressing round
Assess the wound thoroughly, obtain vital sign context, maintain aseptic technique, and report the concerning changes appropriately

questions.rationale: A complete assessment and timely communication are needed. The nurse should continue safe wound care principles and avoid minimizing the findings.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Evaluate pain trend and overall patient condition
Reinforce hand hygiene and aseptic dressing technique
Monitor for increasing drainage, spreading redness, or worsening fever
Document wound findings objectively and accurately
Assume infection is ruled out if there is no heavy drainage yet

questions.rationale: All these actions support early infection recognition and prevention of further deterioration. Heavy drainage is not required for infection to be present.

questions.sectionLabel: Fever, Redness, and Early Wound Infection
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Dressing changes continue without reassessment of symptoms
Documentation is vague and incomplete
The wound changes are reported early, treatment begins if ordered, and the patient shows no progression to more severe infection
The wound becomes more swollen and febrile with no action

questions.rationale: Effective care involves early detection, accurate reporting, and prevention of worsening infection.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which details make this order unsafe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Potassium chloride is a high-alert medication
The potassium level is low but cardiac risk is high
Rapid administration could be lethal
The order states IV push administration
The patient is not yet on cardiac monitoring

questions.rationale: All these elements are clinically significant. While the patient needs replacement, the route and rate are unsafe as written. NCLEX medication safety questions often test recognition of unsafe orders even when treatment itself is necessary.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Because the potassium is low, any route is acceptable if given carefully
The safest plan is to ignore the order completely
The order must be clarified because IV potassium should not be administered by IV push
Rapid potassium replacement is harmless if the patient is awake

questions.rationale: The medication is needed, but the route is unsafe. The nurse must clarify and follow safe infusion practice.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for fatal dysrhythmia due to unsafe medication administration technique
Knowledge deficit about diet
Delayed breakfast

questions.rationale: The immediate priority is prevention of iatrogenic harm from incorrect potassium administration.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the patient whether IV push is acceptable
Hold the unsafe administration, clarify the order, and prepare potassium for controlled infusion according to policy
Give the potassium slowly by hand as IV push
Wait for the next shift to handle it

questions.rationale: The nurse must stop the unsafe process and clarify the order immediately. Controlled infusion and monitoring are essential for safe potassium replacement.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional safety actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an infusion pump for controlled administration
Document the clarification process accurately
Recheck potassium and assess clinical response as ordered
Assume all concentrated electrolytes can be pushed quickly in emergencies
Monitor cardiac rhythm if indicated by policy and patient condition

questions.rationale: These are all correct and reflect high-alert medication safety. Concentrated electrolytes require strict control and should never be treated casually.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates safe management?

options.text: The unsafe order is clarified, potassium is infused correctly, and the patient is monitored without arrhythmic complication
The IV push is given and the patient remains asymptomatic initially
No one documents the near-miss because the patient was not harmed
The order remains unclear but is followed anyway

questions.rationale: Safe management includes preventing harm, correcting the order, and ensuring proper monitoring and documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings are important in a safe pain assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pain score of 8 out of 10
Worsening trend over the last hour
Availability of PRN opioid medication
Guarding and grimacing
Prior borderline low respiratory rate after earlier opioid dosing

questions.rationale: All these findings matter. Pain assessment includes severity, behaviour, trend, available treatment, and safety factors such as respiratory status if opioids may be used.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient has significant pain, but opioid safety assessment must be completed before administration
The pain score alone determines the entire plan
The patient should not receive any pain treatment because he is sleepy
The nurse should give the opioid immediately without reassessment because the patient reports severe pain

questions.rationale: The nurse must address pain while also evaluating sedation, respiration, and medication safety. A high pain score does not eliminate the need for assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for loneliness
Disturbed sleep pattern
Knowledge deficit about surgery
Acute pain requiring intervention balanced with risk for opioid-related oversedation

questions.rationale: The nurse’s priority is a safe plan that treats pain without causing respiratory harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Refuse all pain medication without reassessment
Reassess respiratory rate, sedation level, and full pain context before administering the opioid
Give the opioid immediately because pain is 8 out of 10
Document the pain and return later

questions.rationale: This is the safest first step. In Fundamentals, nurses are expected to assess before they intervene—especially when a high-risk medication such as an opioid is involved.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Consider the timing and response to the previous opioid dose
Assume that severe pain always justifies any opioid dose
Use non-pharmacological comfort measures as appropriate alongside medication planning
Communicate concerns if sedation or respirations make the PRN unsafe
Reassess pain and respiratory status after intervention

questions.rationale: Safe pain care is reassessment-based and individualized. Severe pain does not override respiratory safety concerns.

questions.sectionLabel: Acute Pain Assessment and Safe Intervention
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing management?

options.text: The pain remains uncontrolled because assessment was skipped
Pain improves to a more tolerable level, respiratory status remains safe, and reassessment confirms benefit without oversedation
The nurse gives medication but does not reassess
The patient sleeps heavily and cannot be aroused easily

questions.rationale: Effective management balances symptom relief with patient safety and post-intervention evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings support fluid volume deficit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Persistent vomiting and diarrhea
Dizziness when changing position
Tachycardia
Concentrated urine
Dry mucous membranes

questions.rationale: All these are classic indicators of volume depletion. Orthostatic symptoms and tachycardia suggest the body is compensating for reduced circulating volume.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The vomiting and diarrhea are unrelated to the dizziness
The patient is mainly anxious and should rest
The patient likely has fluid volume deficit with risk for worsening perfusion if untreated
Concentrated urine is unimportant

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster clearly indicates dehydration or volume depletion. Waiting may allow hypotension and poor perfusion to worsen.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Acute boredom
Disturbed sleep pattern
Social isolation
Risk for decreased tissue perfusion related to fluid loss

questions.rationale: Perfusion and circulation are the most urgent concerns in fluid deficit.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the dizziness and focus on diet teaching only
Assess vital signs and hydration status fully, support safety with position changes, and begin fluid replacement measures as ordered
Encourage the patient to walk quickly to improve circulation
Delay intervention until the next set of observations

questions.rationale: The nurse should protect the patient from falls and worsening symptoms while initiating appropriate rehydration and assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor intake and output closely
Assume that because the patient is young, perfusion risk is low
Reassess orthostatic symptoms and pulse after intervention
Provide patient education about slow position changes
Evaluate urine concentration and overall hydration trend

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Younger age does not eliminate the need for careful hydration assessment and safe nursing care.

questions.sectionLabel: Fluid Volume Deficit and Orthostatic Symptoms
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The patient becomes less dizzy, heart rate improves, urine output normalizes, and mucous membranes appear less dry
The nurse documents hydration as improved without reassessment
She becomes more tachycardic and light-headed when sitting up
Intake and output are not monitored

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in better perfusion, better hydration indicators, and symptom relief.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which factors increase this patient’s pressure injury risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limited mobility
Tenderness when moved
Delayed repositioning
Poor nutritional intake
Redness over a pressure area

questions.rationale: All these cues indicate increased risk or early pressure damage. Pressure injuries are often preventable with timely nursing care, making early detection essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Nutrition has no relevance to skin integrity
The patient is beginning to show signs of pressure-related tissue compromise
Stroke patients cannot benefit from repositioning
Redness is harmless if the patient stays in bed

questions.rationale: Persistent pressure-area redness and tenderness suggest early skin compromise. Mobility and nutrition are directly relevant to tissue health.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about reading materials
Social isolation
Risk for impaired skin integrity progressing to pressure injury
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The nurse should prioritise tissue protection and prevention of worsening skin damage.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Massage the area vigorously to improve circulation
Relieve pressure immediately, reposition the patient, and reassess the skin thoroughly
Cover the area without checking it again
Leave the patient in place until the next turn schedule

questions.rationale: Pressure must be relieved quickly. Vigorous massage can worsen tissue damage and is not appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use pressure-relieving devices or surfaces as indicated
Document skin findings objectively
Assume early redness will always resolve without follow-up
Improve communication about repositioning needs among staff
Address nutrition and moisture management

questions.rationale: These interventions reflect good pressure injury prevention practice. Early signs require follow-up, not passive observation.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Redness deepens and no turning plan is changed
Nutrition remains poor and unaddressed
Staff document risk but do not reposition the patient
The area does not worsen, repositioning becomes consistent, and the patient’s skin remains protected

questions.rationale: Effective prevention depends on timely intervention, follow-through, and reassessment.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which factors created wrong-patient medication risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adjacent bed placement
Similar patient surnames
Use of only one identifier
Medications prepared before full bedside verification
Distracted patient response

questions.rationale: All of these factors increased the likelihood of a wrong-patient medication error. Similar names and incomplete identifier use are common safety traps.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient’s nod was enough confirmation
A serious near miss occurred because proper patient identification was not completed
Similar names are unavoidable so no system issue exists
Near misses do not matter if the medication was not given

questions.rationale: Near misses are important because they reveal unsafe processes before harm occurs. Proper identification requires two approved identifiers, not assumptions or distracted confirmation.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Delay in medication round timing
Noise level on the ward
Staff embarrassment
Risk for wrong-patient medication administration due to identification failure

questions.rationale: Preventing wrong-patient medication administration is the priority. Patient identification errors can cause serious harm.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Chart the dose as given and return later
Give the medication because the patient nodded
Ask the roommate to confirm identity
Stop the process and verify identity using two approved identifiers before any medication is administered

questions.rationale: Medication administration must stop until the correct patient is confirmed. Roommates and nods are not valid identifiers.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume that because no harm occurred, no review is needed
Review how bedside verification is performed on the unit
Reinforce safeguards for patients with similar names
Continue using two identifiers consistently for all medications
Report the near miss according to policy

questions.rationale: Near misses should be reported and used for system improvement. Reliable identification is a core Fundamentals safety principle.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Single-identifier practice continues on the ward
Staff dismiss the event because the medications were not actually given
Similar-name safeguards are not reviewed
The error is prevented before administration, reported appropriately, and identification practice is strengthened

questions.rationale: A successful outcome includes both prevention of immediate harm and learning that reduces recurrence.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which factors are important when deciding what to delegate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Scope of the UAP role
Patient stability
Whether teaching is required
Whether assessment or clinical judgment is needed
Complexity and predictability of the task

questions.rationale: All these are delegation essentials. Fundamentals questions often test understanding of right task, right person, and right supervision.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Routine predictable tasks for stable patients may be delegated, but teaching and unstable care remain with the RN
Unstable post-operative care is ideal to delegate because it needs close watching
Any task may be delegated if the RN is busy enough
A UAP may independently teach a new anticoagulant if the RN is nearby

questions.rationale: Delegation is based on patient stability and task complexity. Initial teaching and unstable assessments require RN judgment.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which task is safest to delegate?

options.text: Lunch setup for the stable dialysis patient and routine hygiene care for the stable patient
Interpretation of abnormal vital signs
Assessment of the unstable post-operative patient’s hypotension
Comprehensive discharge teaching about anticoagulation

questions.rationale: Routine predictable tasks for stable patients are appropriate for delegation. Teaching, interpretation, and unstable assessments are not.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the RN do first?

options.text: Match tasks to role scope, give clear directions, and keep unstable/teaching tasks with the RN
Avoid delegation entirely
Delegate everything and sort it out later
Let the UAP decide which patients are stable enough

questions.rationale: Safe delegation requires active RN decision-making and supervision. The RN remains accountable for the delegation choice.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the UAP what findings must be reported immediately
Ensure follow-up and evaluation of delegated tasks
Assume no supervision is needed after delegation
Personally reassess any patient if a concerning change is reported
Keep teaching and unstable clinical judgment tasks with the RN

questions.rationale: Delegation includes communication, supervision, and follow-up. The RN’s accountability does not end once a task is assigned.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective delegation?

options.text: Teaching is omitted because it was delegated poorly
No one knows who is responsible for follow-up
The UAP independently manages unstable hypotension without RN involvement
Stable routine care is completed safely, abnormal findings are reported promptly, and RN-only duties remain with the nurse

questions.rationale: Effective delegation improves efficiency without compromising patient safety or scope of practice.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings suggest delirium rather than stable baseline forgetfulness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Family reporting this is worse than usual
Visual misperceptions
Sudden change in mental status
Pulling at the IV line
Acute medical illness

questions.rationale: All these findings point toward delirium. Acute change, fluctuating confusion, misperceptions, and associated medical illness are important clues.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: This is normal ageing and needs no action
The patient may be experiencing delirium related to acute illness and needs urgent assessment and safety support
Memory loss alone explains the behaviour
The patient is intentionally difficult

questions.rationale: Delirium is a medical-surgical emergency because it often reflects acute physiological disruption and creates injury risk.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired socialization
Deficient recreation
Acute confusion with risk for injury and missed medical deterioration
Chronic low self-esteem

questions.rationale: The patient’s safety and possible underlying medical worsening are the immediate concerns.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reassess medical status, ensure environmental safety, and communicate the acute mental status change promptly
Assume the family is exaggerating
Leave the patient alone to rest in a dark room
Tell the patient firmly to stop hallucinating

questions.rationale: The nurse should respond with assessment, safety, and escalation. Arguing with altered perceptions is not therapeutic.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Involve family for reassurance if appropriate
Gentle reorientation and calm communication
Assessment for infection, pain, dehydration, or medication contributors
Use restraints as the automatic first option
Reduce environmental hazards and increase supervision

questions.rationale: These are appropriate first-line delirium interventions. Restraints are not first choice and should only be considered under strict least-restrictive principles if truly necessary.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The patient becomes safer, underlying causes are addressed, and mental status trends are monitored closely
Family concerns are ignored
Supervision is reduced because she looks tired
The patient is labelled “difficult” with no medical review

questions.rationale: Effective delirium care focuses on safety, reassessment, and treatment of the underlying cause.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which facts make this a documentation safety issue? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient appears comfortable now
Another dose may be considered soon
Timing matters for PRN safety
The nurse is considering charting it as if done earlier
A medication was given but not charted on time

questions.rationale: All of these factors are relevant. The patient’s current comfort does not remove the need for accurate medication timing in the record.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Another nurse can chart it instead
Timing does not matter for PRN medication records
A truthful late entry is required; backdating as if charted in real time would be inappropriate
The medication event should not be documented because it is late

questions.rationale: Late entries should be documented honestly according to policy. Falsifying timing undermines both safety and legal integrity.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Saving time in charting
Preventing staff discussion
Maintaining a truthful record so future medication decisions remain safe
Avoiding embarrassment for the nurse

questions.rationale: The priority is patient safety and record integrity. The next dose decision depends on accurate information.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Omit the record entirely because it is late
Chart the time as if it were entered immediately after administration
Ask a colleague to document it under their login
Enter the medication as a late entry according to policy and communicate the actual administration time clearly

questions.rationale: The correct action is honest late documentation and clear communication to protect safe ongoing care.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clarify the actual administration time to the incoming nurse
Assume the omission has no consequence because the patient is stable
Reflect on workflow improvements to prevent recurrence
Reassess the patient’s current pain status
Follow facility policy for corrections and late entries

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Safe documentation supports safe future care, and prevention of repeated omissions matters.

questions.sectionLabel: Error-Free Documentation and Late Entry Integrity
questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The record reflects an accurate late entry, the handover includes the correct timing, and further medication decisions remain safe
No correction is made because the patient is comfortable
The note is altered to look on time
A second PRN dose is given without knowing the first time

questions.rationale: Effective management protects both the patient and the integrity of the clinical record.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible progression toward sepsis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia and tachypnoea
Falling blood pressure from baseline
Reduced urine output
Fever
New confusion

questions.rationale: All listed findings are important sepsis warning signs. NGN questions often emphasize trend recognition rather than waiting for extreme collapse.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient may be progressing to sepsis and requires urgent reassessment and escalation
The patient is simply tired from pneumonia
The fever should be treated, but the rest can wait
Confusion is unrelated to infection

questions.rationale: The full pattern suggests systemic deterioration, not routine fatigue. Sepsis can worsen rapidly and must be escalated early.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about coughing exercises
Risk for impaired tissue perfusion and organ dysfunction related to sepsis
Disturbed sleep pattern
Social isolation

questions.rationale: The priority is preventing progression of sepsis-related perfusion failure and organ dysfunction.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Focus only on reducing fever with comfort measures
Wait to see whether confusion improves on its own
Escalate urgently, reassess comprehensively, and prepare for sepsis-related interventions according to protocol
Delay communication until routine rounds

questions.rationale: Sepsis management is time-sensitive. Early recognition and escalation improve outcomes.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Communicate the trend clearly using structured handover
Monitor blood pressure, mental status, and urine output closely
Prepare for cultures, fluids, and timely treatment steps as ordered or protocol-based
Assume confusion is unimportant once fever is treated
Watch for worsening respiratory distress

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Confusion is a major sign of deterioration and should not be minimized.

questions.programArea: Building Strong Foundations in Nursing Practice
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing management?

options.text: Sepsis concern is escalated early, treatment begins promptly, and perfusion/mental status trends are followed closely
Hypotension worsens because signs were not reported
Monitoring is reduced after one intervention
Urine output continues falling with no reassessment

questions.rationale: Effective sepsis care depends on early recognition, timely escalation, and ongoing re-evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: Which elements in this scenario create infection transmission risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Contact with wound drainage before assisting the second patient
Moving from one patient to another without hand hygiene
Development of redness and fever later
Contact with IV tubing after contamination risk
Touching the postoperative dressing area

questions.rationale: All of these findings are relevant. The initial lapse in hand hygiene created an infection transmission opportunity, and the later wound findings raise concern that preventable contamination may have occurred. NCLEX safety questions often test the link between a simple omission and later hospital-acquired infection.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation of this event?

options.text: The only important issue is whether antibiotics are ordered
Hand hygiene matters only when gloves are unavailable
Postoperative redness is always normal and unrelated to care
A lapse in standard precautions may have increased the patient’s risk for healthcare-associated infection

questions.rationale: Standard precautions apply to all patient care. Hand hygiene is required before and after patient contact and before clean or aseptic tasks. The nurse should interpret the event as a safety failure with potential infection consequences.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent now?

options.text: Social isolation
Knowledge deficit about exercise
Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for or evidence of wound infection requiring prompt assessment and response

questions.rationale: Once signs of infection appear, the priority becomes prompt assessment and intervention to prevent worsening. The broader systems issue also matters, but the patient’s current safety comes first.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Focus only on apologising to the patient
Ignore the wound because mild fever is common after surgery
Assess the wound and patient comprehensively, perform correct hand hygiene, notify the provider as appropriate, and reinforce infection-prevention practice
Cover the wound without reassessment and wait until tomorrow

questions.rationale: The first step is patient assessment and appropriate escalation. Hand hygiene must be performed correctly going forward, and infection signs must not be dismissed.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document objective findings and actions taken
Use standard precautions consistently even when the exact organism is unknown
Reinforce hand hygiene compliance among staff
Review wound drainage, pain, temperature, and incision appearance
Assume gloves replace hand hygiene in all cases

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate actions. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Safety culture includes honest assessment, documentation, and reinforcement of core precautions.

questions.sectionLabel: Hand Hygiene Failure and Surgical Site Infection Risk
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The wound worsens and no documentation is completed
Staff continue skipping hand hygiene when busy
The wound is assessed early, infection is addressed promptly, and correct hand hygiene practice is consistently followed thereafter
Monitoring stops because one dressing was changed

questions.rationale: Effective management means both immediate patient protection and prevention of repeated lapses through safe practice.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest the need to suspect and isolate for C. difficile? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared bathroom use on the ward
Delay in contact precautions
Additional patients later developing diarrhea
Recent broad-spectrum antibiotic use
Frequent watery diarrhea

questions.rationale: All listed cues are important. Antibiotic exposure and watery diarrhea are classic triggers for suspicion. Shared bathrooms and delayed isolation increase transmission risk.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Isolation should start only after multiple patients are affected
Early contact precautions and environmental control are indicated when C. difficile is suspected
Hand hygiene is unnecessary if gloves are worn
Routine diarrhea care is enough until culture results are final

questions.rationale: Infection control practice prioritises early suspicion and immediate precautions to reduce spread. Waiting for widespread transmission is unsafe.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for transmission of infectious diarrhea to other patients and staff
Social withdrawal
Disturbed sleep pattern
Need for entertainment activities

questions.rationale: Protecting other patients and staff from spread is the immediate safety priority while the symptomatic patient is assessed and treated.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Share equipment freely to save time
Continue routine care until the next shift
Initiate contact precautions promptly, use dedicated equipment, and ensure proper hand hygiene and environmental measures
Move the patient around the ward for observation

questions.rationale: Immediate contact precautions reduce spread. Shared equipment and unnecessary patient movement increase contamination risk.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume alcohol hand rub alone is always sufficient in every C. difficile situation
Wash hands appropriately and follow local policy, especially after glove removal
Use dedicated or disinfected equipment for this patient
Educate staff and visitors about gown and glove use
Reinforce environmental cleaning for contaminated surfaces

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Local policy often emphasises soap-and-water hand hygiene after caring for patients with C. difficile because spores are difficult to remove.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Diarrhea continues spreading because isolation remains delayed
Equipment is shared without cleaning
Staff stop precautions when symptoms lessen slightly
Contact precautions are applied promptly, contamination is reduced, and no further linked spread occurs

questions.rationale: Successful management limits further transmission and applies contact precautions consistently.

questions.stem: Which features should raise suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Night sweats
Weight loss and fatigue
Placement in a shared room before review
Frequent coughing near vulnerable patients
Persistent cough

questions.rationale: All these factors are important. The symptom pattern plus delayed isolation in a shared environment creates a significant airborne transmission concern.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Standard precautions alone are always enough for cough-related illness
Suspected TB should trigger urgent airborne isolation and exposure prevention measures
Airborne precautions can wait until final confirmation
Patient placement matters only after sputum results return

questions.rationale: TB should be managed with a high index of suspicion. Airborne precautions are based on risk, not only final confirmation.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for airborne transmission to other patients and staff
Knowledge deficit about nutrition
Constipation

questions.rationale: Preventing spread to others is the most urgent system-wide safety issue while also supporting the patient’s care.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Arrange airborne isolation immediately, minimise patient movement, and ensure appropriate respiratory protection for staff
Remove all masks to improve patient comfort
Keep the patient in the shared room until all labs return
Encourage the patient to walk around the ward for exercise

questions.rationale: Airborne isolation and staff respiratory protection are key priorities. Delay increases exposure risk.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Consider vulnerable nearby patients in the response plan
Assume cough etiquette alone is enough in suspected TB
Document the time precautions were initiated and actions taken
Limit unnecessary transport and ensure masking as appropriate if transport is required
Communicate clearly about exposure risk and required precautions

questions.rationale: All of these are appropriate. Cough etiquette is helpful but not enough by itself for suspected airborne infection.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The patient remains in a shared room without intervention
The patient is isolated appropriately, staff use correct respiratory protection, and additional exposure risk is reduced
Isolation is delayed until widespread exposure occurs
Vulnerable patients are not considered in planning

questions.rationale: Effective management reduces ongoing transmission risk quickly and systematically.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: Which findings indicate a break in sterile technique? Select all that apply.

options.text: The nurse considered continuing despite contamination
Sterile glove touched a non-sterile bedrail
The dressing change depends on maintaining sterility
The line is an invasive device with infection risk
The procedure involves a central line

questions.rationale: All of these findings matter. Central lines carry serious infection risk, and contamination of sterile gloves means sterility has been broken.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Small contamination can be ignored if the rest of the field looks clean
The sterile field has been compromised and aseptic technique must be re-established
Sterility matters only in operating rooms
Only hand hygiene is relevant during dressing changes

questions.rationale: Asepsis is not partial. Once contamination occurs, the nurse must restore sterility rather than continue with a compromised glove or field.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Anxiety about supplies
Mild inconvenience for the nurse
Risk for catheter-related bloodstream infection due to break in sterile technique
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The patient’s central line creates a direct route for infection, making sterile integrity essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop, replace contaminated sterile equipment or gloves as needed, and re-establish full sterile technique before continuing
Continue quickly before contamination spreads
Touch other supplies to see if they are still sterile
Skip the dressing change entirely and do nothing

questions.rationale: The safest response is to stop and restore asepsis before proceeding. Rushing forward would expose the patient to unnecessary infection risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume contamination is acceptable if no one saw it happen
Reinforce to staff that any break in sterility requires correction
Document the dressing change and patient line status accurately
Assess the site for redness, drainage, or tenderness
Maintain central line infection-prevention standards throughout the procedure

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate responses. Infection prevention depends on consistent correction of breaks in sterile technique, whether or not others observed them.

questions.sectionLabel: Sterile Technique During Central Line Dressing Change
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The nurse continues with contaminated gloves and the site later becomes inflamed
The dressing change is completed with restored sterility, the line site remains clean, and infection risk is minimized
Documentation omits the procedure details
Infection prevention standards are applied inconsistently

questions.rationale: Effective care means restoring sterile technique and protecting the patient from preventable line infection.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: Which findings indicate high fall risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Hidden call bell and bed not optimally positioned
Weak, unsteady gait
Evening agitation
Acute confusion
Repeated attempts to get out of bed unassisted

questions.rationale: All these factors increase fall risk. Cognitive change, poor mobility, environmental setup, and agitation are classic contributors in hospital falls.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient is restless but not at significant risk
The best solution is to ignore the behaviour so she settles down
The patient is at high risk for preventable fall injury and needs immediate safety intervention
Restraints are always the first-line intervention

questions.rationale: This patient has multiple fall risk factors. First-line care should focus on least restrictive safety measures and close observation.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about infection
Disturbed sleep pattern
Social isolation
Risk for injury related to delirium, weakness, and unsafe mobility attempts

questions.rationale: The priority is injury prevention. Falls can lead to major complications in older adults.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Raise the bed higher so staff can reach her more easily
Use restraints immediately without trying alternatives
Make the environment safer immediately, place the bed low, ensure call bell access, increase observation, and assist with toileting and orientation needs
Leave the patient alone until she rings the bell

questions.rationale: The nurse should first address the environment and supervision. A low bed, accessible call bell, and assistance with needs are evidence-based fall prevention steps.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use non-slip footwear and clear pathways
Reassess the cause of confusion and treat contributing medical issues
Provide calm reorientation and frequent rounding
Assume confusion is permanent and cannot be improved
Consider bed alarm use if appropriate to policy

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Delirium may improve when underlying causes are addressed, so reassessment matters.

questions.sectionLabel: Fall Prevention in a Confused Older Adult
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Staff remove the call bell to stop repeated use
Monitoring is reduced because she looks sleepy
She falls overnight because the environment was not adjusted
The patient remains free from falls, receives assistance before mobilising, and becomes somewhat calmer with supportive reorientation

questions.rationale: Effective fall prevention combines environmental measures, observation, and support for the underlying cause of confusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: Which elements make this a significant sharps safety incident? Select all that apply.

options.text: The injury occurred during a distracted workflow moment
Reporting and follow-up may be needed
The patient’s bloodborne risk status may be unknown
A used needle punctured the nurse’s skin
The needle was being recapped

questions.rationale: All of these details matter. Recapping is a known sharps hazard, and even a small puncture requires appropriate exposure management.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Recapping is acceptable if done carefully
Small needle sticks can be ignored if the glove was on
Only the employee’s supervisor needs to know next week
This is an occupational exposure requiring immediate first aid, reporting, and follow-up according to policy

questions.rationale: Gloves reduce but do not eliminate risk. The nurse must treat this as a reportable exposure and follow policy promptly.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for bloodborne pathogen exposure related to sharps injury
Embarrassment about the incident
Delay in lunch break
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The priority is exposure management and prevention of infection-related harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Perform immediate first aid, report the exposure promptly, and follow occupational health or exposure protocol
Recap the needle more carefully next time and do nothing else
Hide the injury because it seems minor
Continue working without telling anyone

questions.rationale: Immediate first aid and reporting are required. Delayed or hidden exposure increases risk and weakens safety culture.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: Which additional safety actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review sharps disposal practices and avoid recapping
Complete required documentation and source/exposed-person follow-up steps
Participate in system review if workflow contributed to the incident
Assume near-misses and minor injuries do not matter
Reinforce use of puncture-resistant sharps containers nearby

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Safety culture depends on learning from both injuries and near-misses.

questions.sectionLabel: Sharps Safety and Needle Stick Exposure
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Recapping continues because the staff are busy
Documentation is avoided to protect reputations
The exposure is addressed promptly, follow-up is completed, and safer sharps handling is reinforced
The injury is hidden and no protocol is followed

questions.rationale: Effective management protects staff, supports legal and occupational requirements, and prevents recurrence.

questions.stem: Which factors create fire or burn risk in this scenario? Select all that apply.

options.text: Petroleum-based product near the face
Electrical heating device near the bed
Oxygen therapy in use
Lack of patient education about oxygen safety
Loose oxygen tubing near linens and equipment

questions.rationale: All of these factors increase hazard in an oxygen-enriched environment. Oxygen supports combustion, petroleum products are unsafe near oxygen, and electrical heat sources add risk.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Lip ointment choice is only a comfort issue
The patient is at increased risk of fire or burn injury and requires immediate environmental safety correction
The setup is safe because oxygen itself does not burn
Electrical devices are always safe if the patient is awake

questions.rationale: Although oxygen is not itself flammable, it greatly increases combustion risk. The setup requires immediate correction.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for fire-related injury in an oxygen-enriched environment
Mild discomfort from dry lips
Disturbed sleep pattern
Knowledge deficit about nutrition

questions.rationale: The immediate threat is environmental fire or burn injury.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove the unsafe items, correct the environment immediately, and educate the patient and family about oxygen precautions
Wait until discharge teaching to mention oxygen safety
Turn the oxygen up higher to compensate for the room setup
Ignore the petroleum product because it is only on the lips

questions.rationale: Safety hazards should be corrected immediately, not later. Oxygen safety education is part of risk reduction.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep ignition sources away from oxygen equipment
Assume family members already know oxygen safety rules
Secure tubing to reduce tangling and environmental hazard
Ensure only approved water-based products are used if needed
Reinforce no-smoking and fire-risk education as appropriate

questions.rationale: These are all correct safety interventions. Education should never be assumed.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The heating device remains because the family prefers it
Education is omitted because no fire has occurred yet
Oxygen tubing stays tangled across the bed
Unsafe products and devices are removed, the patient understands oxygen precautions, and the environment is safer

questions.rationale: Preventing harm is the goal. A safer environment and improved understanding show effective nursing intervention.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest aspiration risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wet voice afterward
Recent stroke
Water given while semi-reclined
No completed swallow assessment yet
Coughing during swallowing

questions.rationale: All listed cues suggest dysphagia and aspiration risk. Stroke can impair swallowing, and coughing with a wet voice after intake is especially concerning.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Family feeding before assessment is harmless
The patient tolerated fluids well
Coughing always means the airway is cleared and there is no problem
The patient may have aspirated and needs immediate swallowing safety intervention

questions.rationale: The nurse must take the event seriously. Aspiration may lead to airway compromise or pneumonia if precautions are not applied.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Social isolation
Risk for aspiration and impaired airway protection
Low self-esteem
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: Airway protection comes first in a patient with suspected swallowing impairment.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the family to continue helping because they mean well
Delay assessment until meal time
Stop oral intake, assess the patient’s respiratory status, position safely, and ensure formal swallowing precautions are followed
Offer more water to test tolerance

questions.rationale: The nurse must stop unsafe oral intake and protect the airway immediately. Family intention does not change the aspiration risk.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clarify NPO status and swallow orders with the team
Educate the family about why unapproved oral intake is unsafe
Monitor for coughing, choking, wet voice, or respiratory change
Maintain upright positioning during any allowed intake
Assume aspiration risk ends once the coughing stops

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Aspiration complications may continue even after immediate coughing subsides.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Positioning is ignored during future meals
Oral intake is withheld until safe, aspiration signs do not recur, and the family understands swallowing precautions
The patient develops worsening respiratory symptoms without reassessment
Water continues to be offered because the patient is thirsty

questions.rationale: Effective care prevents repeat aspiration and improves family understanding of safety precautions.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.stem: Which findings indicate increased pressure injury risk or early injury? Select all that apply.

options.text: Immobility after stroke
Warmth at pressure area
Repositioning delays
Poor nutritional intake
Non-blanching redness over sacrum

questions.rationale: All listed findings are relevant. Immobility, delayed turning, poor nutrition, and early skin changes are classic pressure injury concerns.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Pressure injuries occur only in ICU patients
The skin changes are insignificant and can be reviewed later
Early pressure injury is developing and immediate prevention/escalation measures are required
Warm skin means circulation is fine and there is no issue

questions.rationale: The patient is showing early pressure damage. Prompt intervention can prevent progression.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Need for reading materials
Disturbed sleep
Social withdrawal
Risk for worsening tissue injury related to sustained pressure and impaired mobility

questions.rationale: Tissue preservation is the immediate priority. Delay may convert an early injury into a deeper wound.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Massage the reddened area vigorously
Cover the area without reassessment
Leave the patient in the same position until morning
Relieve pressure immediately, reposition the patient, assess the skin thoroughly, and update the prevention plan

questions.rationale: Pressure must be relieved immediately. Vigorous massage can worsen tissue damage and is not appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Pressure Injury Prevention in an Immobile Patient
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document skin findings precisely
Address nutrition and moisture management
Use pressure-relieving surfaces or devices as indicated
