Delay intervention until the next prenatal visit
Begin focused assessment of hydration status, support rest, and prepare for fluid replacement and antiemetic therapy as prescribed
Tell the patient that vomiting is normal and she should go home

questions.rationale: Immediate nursing care should focus on hydration, safety, and preparation for treatment. Forcing a heavy meal is unrealistic and may worsen symptoms. Sending the patient home without treatment would ignore signs of dehydration and clinical deterioration.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor intake and output closely
Observe for worsening dizziness or electrolyte-related weakness
Reassess weight trends and urine concentration
Provide nonjudgmental support and explain the condition
Ignore emotional distress because physical issues are the only priority

questions.rationale: NGN-level maternity care includes both physical and emotional support. Intake/output and weight trends help evaluate hydration and nutrition. Emotional reassurance matters because prolonged vomiting can be frightening and discouraging. Ignoring distress would not reflect holistic nursing care.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the plan of care is effective?

options.text: The patient tolerates fluids better, urine becomes less concentrated, pulse slows, and dizziness decreases
Vomiting worsens and the patient becomes more hypotensive
The nurse stops monitoring after one dose of antiemetic
The patient remains unable to take in fluids but says she feels hopeful

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better hydration, less concentrated urine, more stable vital signs, and reduced dizziness. Hopefulness is valuable, but physiological improvement is the clearest outcome indicator.

questions.stem: Which findings are red flags for severe preeclampsia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe headache
Right upper quadrant discomfort
Blood pressure 168/112 mmHg
Visual disturbance
Proteinuria and brisk reflexes

questions.rationale: All of these are classic warning signs of severe preeclampsia. Headache, visual disturbance, and hypertension suggest cerebral involvement. Brisk reflexes indicate increased neuromuscular irritability, and right upper quadrant pain may reflect hepatic involvement. NCLEX-style maternity questions place heavy emphasis on recognising these as urgent findings.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: Severe preeclampsia with risk of seizure, placental compromise, and maternal organ injury
Normal third-trimester discomforts
Early postpartum haemorrhage
Simple anxiety about labour

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster is highly concerning for severe preeclampsia. This is not an expected discomfort of pregnancy. The nurse must think about maternal cerebral, renal, hepatic, and placental risks.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for maternal seizure and reduced placental perfusion
Knowledge deficit regarding breastfeeding
Anxiety about motherhood

questions.rationale: The priority is prevention of maternal and fetal injury. Preeclampsia threatens the brain, liver, kidneys, and uteroplacental circulation. That risk overrides all long-term teaching needs.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk around to reduce swelling
Delay intervention until laboratory results return next day
Offer a large meal and discharge home
Reduce stimulation, maintain safety, initiate close maternal-fetal monitoring, and prepare for urgent antihypertensive and magnesium sulfate therapy as prescribed

questions.rationale: The nurse must reduce seizure risk, support close monitoring, and prepare for time-sensitive management. Walking, discharge, or delay would be unsafe. In severe preeclampsia, nursing priorities include seizure precautions, fetal assessment, and readiness for urgent escalation.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor reflexes, respiratory status, and urine output closely if magnesium sulfate is started
Prepare for possible urgent birth if maternal or fetal status worsens
Maintain a calm, low-stimulation environment
Dismiss blurred vision because oedema alone explains it
Assess fetal heart rate patterns and maternal symptoms frequently

questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate monitoring is critical because toxicity can depress respirations. Fetal monitoring remains essential because placental perfusion may be impaired. Visual changes should never be dismissed in preeclampsia. Anticipating possible urgent delivery reflects advanced clinical judgment.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement or stabilisation?

options.text: Headache intensifies and blood pressure rises further
Fetal monitoring is discontinued because the mother feels calmer
Blood pressure becomes better controlled, severe headache lessens, reflexes are appropriately monitored, and fetal status remains reassuring
Respirations fall dangerously on magnesium sulfate without reassessment

questions.rationale: Stabilisation is shown by improved blood pressure, reduced neurological symptoms, and continued maternal-fetal monitoring. Respiratory depression or worsening hypertension would indicate poor control or complications.

questions.stem: What makes this an obstetric emergency? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pregnancy at 35 weeks
Tonic-clonic seizure activity
Possible fetal compromise during maternal seizure
Known severe preeclampsia
Maternal risk of airway compromise and trauma

questions.rationale: A seizure in a patient with severe preeclampsia is eclampsia, a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Pregnancy context is important, but what makes the situation emergent is the direct risk to maternal airway, oxygenation, circulation, and fetal wellbeing.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s priority interpretation?

options.text: The patient is having a normal labour event
The patient only needs comfort measures
The patient is experiencing eclampsia requiring immediate seizure management and maternal-fetal stabilisation
The seizure can be ignored until it stops

questions.rationale: This is eclampsia and must be treated urgently. NCLEX expects immediate recognition of seizure risk in hypertensive pregnancy complications and rapid implementation of emergency priorities.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent during the seizure?

options.text: Airway obstruction, maternal injury, and decreased oxygen delivery to mother and fetus
Need for postpartum teaching
Anxiety about labour pain
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: During active seizure, the greatest danger is compromise of maternal airway, oxygenation, and physical safety. The fetus is also vulnerable if maternal oxygen delivery drops.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Try to hold the patient down forcefully
Leave the room to find the doctor before doing anything else
Stay with the patient, protect from injury, position for airway safety as feasible after the seizure, call for urgent help, and prepare prescribed seizure management
Put an object in the patient’s mouth to prevent tongue injury

questions.rationale: The nurse must remain with the patient, protect from injury, and support airway safety. Objects should never be forced into the mouth. Forceful restraint can injure the patient. Leaving the room without first ensuring active response and protection would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate after the seizure subsides? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain seizure precautions and low stimulation
Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, and maternal level of consciousness
Assess fetal status and continue close monitoring
Assume no further assessment is needed once the shaking stops
Prepare for magnesium sulfate or review of ongoing magnesium therapy as ordered

questions.rationale: Post-seizure care includes full maternal reassessment, fetal reassessment, seizure prevention strategies, and medication management. The end of visible seizure activity does not mean the emergency has ended.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that immediate nursing management is effective?

options.text: The nurse documents only the duration without reassessment
Fetal status is ignored because the seizure is over
The patient remains unmonitored after the seizure ends
The mother is protected from injury, airway is maintained, maternal status is reassessed, and fetal monitoring resumes appropriately

questions.rationale: Effective care includes protection during the seizure and comprehensive reassessment afterward. Both mother and fetus require continued evaluation.

questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with placenta previa? Select all that apply.

options.text: Absence of abdominal pain
Ongoing fetal movement
Painless bleeding
Bright-red vaginal bleeding
Third-trimester presentation

questions.rationale: Placenta previa typically presents with painless bright-red bleeding in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal movement may still be present, especially if fetal compromise has not yet developed. The absence of pain helps distinguish it from placental abruption in many cases.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Postpartum haemorrhage
Likely placenta previa requiring maternal-fetal assessment and bleeding precautions
Placental abruption with severe pain
Normal labour show

questions.rationale: The bleeding pattern strongly suggests placenta previa. Because placenta overlies or approaches the cervical os, vaginal bleeding may occur without pain. The nurse must think about safe assessment and preventing further bleeding.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about newborn sleep
Readiness for discharge
Disturbed body image
Risk for maternal blood loss and fetal compromise related to placental bleeding

questions.rationale: The immediate concern is ongoing bleeding and its impact on maternal circulation and fetal perfusion.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess maternal-fetal status, monitor bleeding, and avoid vaginal examination until placenta location is confirmed by the appropriate team
Perform a digital vaginal exam to check dilation
Delay fetal monitoring until bleeding stops
Encourage the patient to walk around

questions.rationale: In suspected placenta previa, digital vaginal examination may provoke severe bleeding and is contraindicated unless specifically directed in a controlled setting. Maternal and fetal monitoring are immediate priorities.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor vital signs and bleeding amount closely
Explain the need for pelvic rest if ordered
Prepare for ultrasound-based evaluation and possible admission
Ignore maternal anxiety because bleeding is the only priority
Apply fetal monitoring and assess fetal status

questions.rationale: Maternity care is both physiological and supportive. Monitoring, fetal assessment, preparation for evaluation, and patient teaching are all appropriate. Anxiety should not be ignored.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates stable management at this stage?

options.text: A digital exam is performed without indication
Bleeding decreases or remains controlled, maternal vital signs stay stable, and fetal status remains reassuring
The patient is discharged without ongoing assessment
Bleeding increases while monitoring is reduced

questions.rationale: Stable maternal signs and reassuring fetal assessment indicate the situation is under better control, though continued vigilance is still needed.

questions.stem: Which findings support placental abruption? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dark vaginal bleeding
Uterine tenderness and firmness
Reduced fetal movement
Signs of maternal instability
Severe abdominal pain

questions.rationale: Placental abruption typically presents with painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, and often reduced fetal movement due to compromised placental exchange. Maternal tachycardia and hypotension suggest significant blood loss or shock.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Baby blues
Normal labour discomfort
Placental abruption with risk of maternal haemorrhage and fetal compromise
Placenta previa

questions.rationale: This is a painful bleeding emergency, unlike the typically painless bleeding seen with placenta previa. The nurse must recognise the dual risk to mother and fetus.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired placental perfusion with maternal haemorrhage risk
Knowledge deficit about parenting
Disturbed sleep pattern
Need for menu planning

questions.rationale: Placental separation compromises fetal oxygenation and may lead to severe maternal bleeding. This is a high-priority obstetric emergency.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay fetal monitoring until the bleeding is measured for several hours
Encourage the patient to walk to the toilet
Offer oral food and fluids first
Initiate urgent maternal-fetal assessment, support circulation, and prepare for emergency obstetric management

questions.rationale: The nurse must stabilise maternal circulation and monitor fetal status immediately. Delay or unnecessary activity would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Preparation for urgent birth if maternal or fetal instability worsens
Continuous fetal heart rate assessment
Maintaining IV access and readiness for rapid intervention as ordered
Frequent monitoring of maternal vital signs and bleeding
Assuming that reduced fetal movement is not important

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement is highly significant and should not be ignored. The nurse must prepare for escalation and possible urgent delivery.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the patient is being effectively stabilised while definitive care is arranged?

options.text: Monitoring is stopped because pain is present
Bleeding increases without reassessment
Maternal perfusion is supported, fetal status is continuously assessed, and the team is prepared for rapid obstetric intervention
The patient is left alone because the doctor has been called

questions.rationale: Effective emergency nursing care involves continuous assessment, support, and anticipation of urgent obstetric management.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: Which description best identifies late decelerations?

options.text: Decelerations that begin after the contraction peak and recover after the contraction ends
A reassuring fetal pattern
Decelerations that mirror the contraction exactly
Abrupt drops associated with cord compression

questions.rationale: Late decelerations start after the peak of the contraction and recover after it ends. This timing is the key identifying feature and usually reflects impaired uteroplacental perfusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of repeated late decelerations?

options.text: Normal pushing pattern
Reassuring fetal adaptation
Fetal oxygenation concern related to uteroplacental insufficiency
Maternal anxiety only

questions.rationale: Late decelerations are abnormal because they suggest the fetus is not tolerating contractions well, often due to decreased oxygen transfer.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Room temperature discomfort
Need for breastfeeding education
Maternal boredom
Potential fetal compromise due to reduced placental oxygen exchange

questions.rationale: The fetus is the most immediate concern here. The nurse must intervene to improve oxygen delivery and reduce stress on the fetus.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the mother to push harder
Delay action until the next shift
Reposition the mother, reduce or stop oxytocin as indicated by protocol, support oxygenation, and increase maternal-fetal assessment
Leave the oxytocin unchanged and ignore the tracing

questions.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation measures include maternal repositioning, addressing oxytocin-driven uterine stress, supporting oxygenation, and close monitoring. This is a classic NCLEX maternity priority question.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare for further intervention if the pattern persists
Assess maternal blood pressure and contraction pattern
Consider an IV fluid bolus if indicated or ordered
Notify the provider or midwife of the non-reassuring pattern
Continue to label the pattern as normal to calm the patient

questions.rationale: The nurse must address reversible causes and escalate appropriately. Falsely labelling the pattern as normal would be unsafe and misleading.

questions.sectionLabel: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the interventions are effective?

options.text: Decelerations worsen while oxytocin continues unchanged
The mother remains uninformed and distressed
Fetal tracing is not reassessed after repositioning
Late decelerations reduce or resolve and fetal tracing becomes more reassuring

questions.rationale: The goal of intervention is a more reassuring fetal pattern. The nurse must evaluate whether intrauterine resuscitation is working and escalate if it is not.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible cord prolapse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Abrupt severe decelerations
Ongoing non-reassuring fetal tracing
Sudden fetal bradycardia after rupture of membranes
Need for rapid intrauterine resuscitation
Timing immediately after membranes rupture

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse is classically suspected when severe fetal heart rate compromise occurs immediately after rupture of membranes. The sequence of events is highly important in the diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Probable umbilical cord compression/prolapse causing acute fetal hypoxia risk
Reassuring labour progression
Normal maternal anxiety response
Postpartum complication

questions.rationale: The problem is urgent fetal compromise from cord compression. NCLEX expects immediate recognition because delay can be catastrophic.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Maternal sleep deprivation
Acute interruption of fetal oxygen delivery due to cord compression
Breastfeeding readiness
Need for newborn bath preparation

questions.rationale: The fetus is at immediate risk because the compressed cord limits oxygenated blood flow.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the patient to find paperwork first
Delay intervention until contractions slow
Call for help, relieve pressure from the presenting part as indicated, reposition the patient urgently, and prepare for emergency birth
Encourage the patient to sit upright and push

questions.rationale: Relieving cord compression and summoning urgent obstetric help are the priorities. Time is critical, and the nurse must act immediately.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clear communication with the patient and team
Assuming the tracing will normalise without action
Continuous fetal monitoring
Preparation for urgent operative birth if indicated
Maintaining interventions that reduce cord compression

questions.rationale: Every minute matters in cord prolapse. Ongoing monitoring, communication, decompression, and preparation for emergency birth are all correct.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that nursing management is helping while definitive delivery is arranged?

options.text: Fetal heart rate improves or is better maintained while pressure is relieved and the team prepares for urgent birth
The patient is left uninformed and alone
No further monitoring is done after the first response
Fetal tracing worsens while interventions are stopped

questions.rationale: Improved or better-maintained fetal status while emergency delivery is organised shows that decompression efforts are helping.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest shoulder dystocia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retraction of the fetal head against the perineum
Risk of fetal hypoxia and birth injury
Need for urgent manoeuvres
Head delivers but shoulders do not follow
Birth process suddenly stalls

questions.rationale: These findings strongly indicate shoulder dystocia. The retraction of the head, often called the turtle sign, is a classic cue.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Shoulder dystocia requiring immediate coordinated obstetric manoeuvres
Normal labour delay
Postpartum haemorrhage
Placenta previa

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency because the impacted shoulder can prevent delivery and compromise fetal oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Need for discharge teaching
Risk for fetal hypoxia and traumatic birth injury
Sleep deprivation
Maternal thirst

questions.rationale: The urgency lies in relieving the shoulder impaction to allow delivery and prevent hypoxia or injury.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the room to call family
Pull forcefully on the fetal head
Call for help immediately and assist with emergency manoeuvres according to the provider’s direction
Delay action until the next contraction

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires immediate team response and use of recognised manoeuvres. Forceful traction can cause serious injury and is inappropriate.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare equipment and personnel for neonatal assessment after birth
Maintain calm communication with the team
Provide clear, focused support to the mother
Anticipate possible maternal trauma or postpartum bleeding after delivery
Assume the infant will always be fine after delivery

questions.rationale: The nurse must think beyond the moment of delivery and anticipate neonatal and maternal complications. Calm teamwork is essential.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective emergency management?

options.text: The nurse stops monitoring after the infant is born
Delivery remains stalled with no coordinated response
Maternal assessment is ignored after delivery
The infant is delivered, immediate neonatal assessment occurs, and the mother is assessed for trauma and bleeding

questions.rationale: Successful management includes safe delivery and immediate follow-up care for both mother and infant.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: Which findings indicate postpartum haemorrhage with uterine atony? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heavy vaginal bleeding
Dizziness and weakness
Pallor
Boggy enlarged uterus
Tachycardia and low blood pressure

questions.rationale: These are hallmark findings of postpartum haemorrhage. A boggy uterus suggests uterine atony, one of the most common causes of PPH. Hemodynamic changes show significant blood loss.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Retained urine only
Postpartum haemorrhage likely caused by uterine atony
Normal postpartum lochia
Normal fatigue after delivery

questions.rationale: This bleeding exceeds normal lochia and is associated with a soft, enlarged uterus and unstable vital signs. NCLEX maternity care requires rapid recognition of uterine atony as an emergency.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for hypovolemic shock from postpartum blood loss
Need for infant bathing teaching
Mild discomfort from contractions
Sleep deprivation

questions.rationale: Severe blood loss threatens maternal perfusion and can lead quickly to shock. That is the immediate priority.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Focus only on breastfeeding support
Send the patient to shower
Massage the fundus, call for assistance, assess bleeding, and prepare uterotonic therapy as prescribed
Delay action because bleeding is common after birth

questions.rationale: Fundal massage and urgent support are initial priorities in uterine atony. The nurse must not minimise heavy bleeding because postpartum haemorrhage can deteriorate rapidly.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare IV fluids and medications as ordered
Continue to assess lochia and uterine tone
Monitor vital signs frequently
Ignore the patient’s dizziness if bleeding seems to slow briefly
Evaluate bladder distention because a full bladder can worsen atony

questions.rationale: PPH requires repeated reassessment. Bladder distention can interfere with uterine contraction. Dizziness remains clinically important and should not be dismissed.

questions.sectionLabel: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Monitoring stops because the fundus was massaged once
The uterus becomes firm, bleeding decreases, vital signs begin to stabilise, and the patient feels less dizzy
The uterus remains boggy and bleeding continues
The patient becomes more hypotensive without escalation

questions.rationale: A firm fundus, reduced bleeding, and improved hemodynamic status show effective control of uterine atony.

questions.stem: Which findings support endometritis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Uterine tenderness
Foul-smelling lochia
Fever
Chills and malaise
Tachycardia

questions.rationale: All findings are consistent with postpartum uterine infection. Risk factors include prolonged labour and invasive or operative birth.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Baby blues
Normal postpartum healing
Breast engorgement only
Postpartum endometritis requiring prompt treatment

questions.rationale: The symptoms suggest uterine infection, not normal recovery. Prompt treatment is needed to prevent progression to sepsis.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Minor perineal discomfort
Disturbed sleep
Infection with risk of systemic spread
Need for newborn bath education

questions.rationale: The main concern is infection and possible systemic deterioration if untreated.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay treatment until fever is rechecked tomorrow
Ignore the odour because lochia can vary
Assess thoroughly, obtain needed cultures as ordered, and prepare for prescribed antibiotic therapy while monitoring maternal status
Encourage discharge home immediately

questions.rationale: The nurse should support timely diagnosis and treatment. Foul-smelling lochia and uterine tenderness are not normal findings to dismiss.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Watch for worsening signs of sepsis
Assess lochia and uterine tenderness trends
Encourage hydration and rest as clinically appropriate
Monitor temperature and vital signs closely
Ignore the patient’s pain if antibiotics are started

questions.rationale: Close monitoring remains important even after treatment starts. Pain and sepsis risk both require ongoing reassessment.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Fever decreases, lochia becomes less offensive, uterine tenderness lessens, and the patient feels stronger
Tachycardia worsens with ongoing pain
No reassessment occurs after antibiotics begin
Fever rises and confusion develops

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduction in infection signs and better overall maternal wellbeing.

questions.stem: Which findings are concerning for significant newborn respiratory distress? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retractions
Nasal flaring
Grunting
Laboured breathing
Central cyanosis

questions.rationale: All of these signs indicate increased work of breathing and poor oxygenation. Unlike benign transitional findings such as acrocyanosis, central cyanosis and significant respiratory effort are urgent.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Newborn respiratory distress requiring immediate assessment and support
Simple hunger cues
Normal newborn transition only
Mild sleepiness

questions.rationale: This infant is not transitioning normally. The pattern strongly indicates respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed parent-infant bonding only
Impaired oxygenation and ineffective breathing in the newborn
Need for routine feeding
Bathing delay

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing always come first, especially in the newborn, who can deteriorate rapidly.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Initiate immediate newborn respiratory assessment and support according to neonatal protocol, and escalate urgently
Swaddle tightly and wait an hour
Feed the infant first
Assume cyanosis will resolve without reassessment

questions.rationale: The nurse must act immediately because this infant shows clear signs of respiratory distress. Delay may lead to severe hypoxia.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Observe for worsening grunting or apnea
Ignore retractions if the infant is term
Maintain thermoregulation while respiratory support is organised
Reassess colour, respiratory effort, and oxygenation frequently
Communicate clearly with the parent while continuing urgent care

questions.rationale: Respiratory distress management includes warmth, reassessment, communication, and observation for worsening fatigue or apnea. Term status does not make retractions normal.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
Cyanosis persists and respirations become weaker
Colour improves, grunting decreases, breathing becomes easier, and the infant maintains better oxygenation
The infant becomes more lethargic without escalation

questions.rationale: Improved work of breathing and oxygenation indicate effective early management.

questions.stem: Which findings support neonatal hypoglycaemia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Poor feeding
Sleepiness/lethargy
Low glucose reading
Jitteriness
Infant of a mother with gestational diabetes

questions.rationale: All of these factors support neonatal hypoglycaemia. Infants of diabetic mothers are at particular risk because of altered glucose-insulin adaptation after birth.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Benign sleep cycle
Mild cold stress alone
Neonatal hypoglycaemia requiring prompt treatment and reassessment
Normal newborn behaviour only

questions.rationale: Low glucose with symptoms must be treated promptly. Waiting risks worsening neurological compromise.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed family sleep
Inadequate glucose availability to the newborn brain
Delayed bathing
Need for routine discharge teaching

questions.rationale: In neonatal hypoglycaemia, neurological protection is the main priority.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Bathe the infant before feeding
Delay action until the next routine blood sugar check
Ignore symptoms if the infant is warm
Initiate feeding or other protocol-based glucose support promptly and reassess the infant closely

questions.rationale: Rapid correction and close reassessment are required. Hypoglycaemia should not be left untreated simply because the infant looks otherwise stable.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Recheck glucose after treatment according to protocol
Assume one low reading is never important
Explain the situation calmly to the parents
Maintain warmth and reduce energy expenditure
Monitor feeding effectiveness and tone

questions.rationale: Thermoregulation, repeat glucose testing, feeding assessment, and parent communication are all appropriate. A low symptomatic reading is always important.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The infant becomes weaker without escalation
Lethargy worsens and feeding remains poor
Monitoring stops after one feed
Glucose rises to a safer range, feeding improves, jitteriness resolves, and the infant becomes more alert

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in both biochemical correction and clinical behaviour.

questions.stem: Which findings support clinically important neonatal jaundice? Select all that apply.

options.text: Need to assess feeding pattern
Increased sleepiness
Yellow discoloration of skin and sclera
Elevated bilirubin level
Newborn age of 3 days

questions.rationale: All the listed points matter. Jaundice is common in newborns, but rising bilirubin plus sleepiness and feeding concerns can indicate a need for treatment and close monitoring.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The infant has postpartum depression
The infant may have clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring monitoring and possibly phototherapy
The colour change is unrelated to bilirubin
This can never be significant because jaundice is always normal

questions.rationale: Physiologic jaundice may be common, but significant bilirubin elevation can be harmful. The nurse must assess severity and follow treatment thresholds.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Umbilical cord stump education only
Risk for bilirubin-related neurological injury if levels rise further
Need for routine bathing advice
Disturbed sleep pattern of the parents

questions.rationale: Very high bilirubin can become dangerous, so preventing neurological injury is the priority.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop feeding the infant
Assess feeding and elimination, verify bilirubin trends, and prepare for phototherapy or other management as ordered
Ignore sleepiness if the infant is yellow
Delay all care until the next day

questions.rationale: Feeding and bilirubin trend assessment are crucial because poor intake can worsen jaundice. Delaying care or stopping feeds would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume jaundice will always resolve without follow-up
Observe for worsening lethargy or poor feeding
Reassess bilirubin according to protocol
Monitor hydration and feeding effectiveness
Provide parent education about jaundice and phototherapy if used

questions.rationale: Safe newborn care includes monitoring, education, and follow-up. A passive wait-and-see approach is inappropriate when bilirubin is already elevated.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Bilirubin trends down, feeding improves, and the infant is more alert
Sleepiness increases and feeding declines
Phototherapy is started but never reassessed
Parents remain uninformed about warning signs

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by falling bilirubin and better feeding/alertness.

questions.stem: Which findings raise concern for neonatal sepsis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Mottling and grunting
Poor feeding
Lethargy
Prolonged rupture of membranes
Temperature instability

questions.rationale: All these findings are concerning. Neonatal sepsis often presents with non-specific signs, so nurses must respond quickly to subtle deterioration.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Mild jaundice only
Possible neonatal sepsis requiring urgent evaluation and treatment
Benign adaptation
Normal newborn tiredness

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster plus prolonged rupture of membranes makes infection a serious concern.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Parent inconvenience
Risk for overwhelming infection and respiratory compromise in the newborn
Need for discharge teaching
Delayed infant bath

questions.rationale: Newborn sepsis can become life-threatening quickly. The priority is survival and prevention of rapid decline.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Escalate urgently, support thermoregulation and respiratory assessment, and prepare for sepsis evaluation and treatment as ordered
Wait to see whether the infant perks up after sleep
Feed only when convenient later
Stop monitoring because the baby is quiet

questions.rationale: Urgent action is required because newborn sepsis may progress rapidly. Thermoregulation and respiratory support are important immediate priorities.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support family understanding while urgent care continues
Ignore grunting if the infant is term
Anticipate cultures and antibiotic therapy as ordered
Monitor colour, tone, respirations, and feeding closely
Reassess temperature and perfusion frequently

questions.rationale: Close observation and family communication are important. Grunting is a serious respiratory sign and must not be ignored.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Lethargy deepens and grunting worsens
Perfusion is not reassessed
Feeding improves, colour and tone stabilise, temperature becomes more consistent, and respiratory effort eases
Monitoring stops after antibiotics start

questions.rationale: Improvement must be seen in behaviour, temperature, perfusion, and breathing.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: Which findings support respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Grunting and nasal flaring
Retractions
Reduced physiological reserve
Tachypnoea
Prematurity at 32 weeks

questions.rationale: Prematurity strongly predisposes to surfactant deficiency and RDS. The visible work of breathing confirms respiratory compromise.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Normal newborn transition only
Benign feeding difficulty
Respiratory distress syndrome requiring close support of breathing and thermoregulation
Stable sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The infant’s prematurity and clear respiratory distress signs indicate RDS rather than normal transition.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Delayed naming ceremony
Need for routine cord teaching only
Impaired gas exchange and risk of worsening fatigue in the premature infant
Parent fatigue

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are always first, especially in preterm infants who fatigue quickly.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the grunting because preterm infants are noisy
Delay intervention to allow longer skin-to-skin time only
Bathe the infant immediately
Support airway and breathing according to neonatal protocol, maintain thermoregulation, and escalate for advanced neonatal management

questions.rationale: The infant requires respiratory and thermal support immediately. Delay may worsen hypoxia and exhaustion.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support parent understanding while urgent care continues
Prepare for neonatal respiratory support measures as ordered
Minimise energy expenditure and unnecessary stimulation
Assume the infant will self-correct without reassessment
Reassess colour, work of breathing, and oxygenation frequently

questions.rationale: A preterm infant with RDS needs close reassessment, energy conservation, and timely escalation. Parent communication remains important.

questions.sectionLabel: Preterm Infant with Respiratory Distress Syndrome
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Temperature falls further without action
Retractions worsen and the infant becomes more lethargic
Monitoring stops once the infant is quieter
Respiratory effort lessens, oxygenation improves, and the infant maintains temperature and colour more effectively

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by easier breathing, better oxygenation, and more stable thermal control.

questions.stem: Which findings most strongly indicate significant respiratory distress in this infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nasal flaring
Poor feeding
Respiratory rate 62 breaths per minute
Oxygen saturation 89% on room air
Subcostal retractions

questions.rationale: All listed findings indicate clinically important respiratory distress. Infants often show deterioration through feeding difficulty, increased work of breathing, tachypnoea, and falling oxygen saturation. NGN paediatric reasoning requires the nurse to see poor feeding not just as a comfort issue, but as a sign of reduced respiratory reserve and fatigue.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of the infant’s condition?

options.text: Normal infant crying pattern
Mild upper respiratory infection only
Bronchiolitis with increasing respiratory effort and risk of deterioration
Isolated gastrointestinal upset

questions.rationale: This is more than a mild viral cold. The infant has a lower respiratory process with increased work of breathing, poor feeding, and low oxygen saturation. Bronchiolitis can worsen quickly in infants because of their small airways and limited reserve.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for impaired gas exchange related to airway inflammation and increased secretions
Parent anxiety alone
Risk for constipation

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are the top priorities. Parent anxiety matters, but the immediate threat is respiratory compromise and potential exhaustion.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay intervention until the next routine observation round
Place the infant flat to promote rest
Force a full bottle feed immediately
Support airway and breathing, position the infant appropriately, monitor oxygenation closely, and prepare for oxygen and suction as indicated by policy or orders

questions.rationale: The first action is to support breathing. Positioning, oxygen assessment, and suction readiness are key interventions in bronchiolitis. Forcing oral intake may worsen distress, and lying flat can compromise breathing further.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor hydration and number of wet nappies
Provide calm explanation and involve the caregiver in ongoing observation
Reassess for worsening fatigue or apnea
Teach the parent to ignore retractions if wheeze is present
Use small frequent feeds only if the infant can tolerate them safely

questions.rationale: Hydration monitoring is important because infants can dehydrate quickly when feeding is poor. Worsening fatigue or apnea may indicate impending failure. Parent education is essential. Retractions should never be ignored.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Respiratory effort decreases, feeding tolerance improves, oxygen saturation rises, and the infant appears less fatigued
Monitoring is stopped because the infant is quieter
Wet nappies remain low and feeding stops completely
Retractions worsen and the infant becomes harder to rouse

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by easier breathing, better oxygenation, and improved feeding and hydration. A quieter infant is not always reassuring if fatigue is increasing.

questions.stem: Which findings are most concerning for dehydration? Select all that apply.

options.text: One small wet nappy only
Less active behaviour
No tears when crying
Tachycardia
Dry lips and sunken eyes

questions.rationale: All listed findings suggest dehydration. In toddlers, behaviour change is especially important. Reduced tears, poor urine output, dry mucosa, tachycardia, and decreased activity indicate fluid volume deficit.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Clinically significant dehydration requiring prompt rehydration support
Normal toddler tantrum behaviour
Mild food refusal with no fluid deficit
Constipation only

questions.rationale: This child shows both physical and behavioural signs of dehydration. NCLEX paediatric questions often require recognising dehydration early before shock develops.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Deficient fluid volume with risk of worsening perfusion
Disturbed sleep
Knowledge deficit about play
Stranger anxiety

questions.rationale: The urgent issue is fluid volume deficit. Dehydration in young children can progress quickly to shock.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Send the child home without assessment
Give solid food immediately
Assess severity carefully, support oral or IV rehydration based on tolerance and orders, and continue close monitoring
Delay fluids until vomiting fully stops for a day

questions.rationale: Rehydration is the key nursing priority. Some children can tolerate oral rehydration; others may require IV therapy. Delay increases risk.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess capillary refill and general responsiveness
Monitor for worsening lethargy or inability to drink
Educate caregivers about small frequent rehydration amounts
Ignore weight change because scales vary
Track intake and output closely

questions.rationale: Intake, output, perfusion, and responsiveness are essential indicators in paediatric dehydration. Caregiver teaching is crucial. Weight changes are clinically important and should not be dismissed.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The toddler becomes more alert, urine output improves, mucous membranes look moist, and heart rate begins to normalise
No wet nappy is produced for several more hours
The nurse stops reassessing because vomiting decreased once
The child becomes more lethargic and capillary refill worsens

questions.rationale: Improvement in hydration is shown by better perfusion, better behaviour, moist mucosa, and improved urine output.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate a significant asthma exacerbation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Repeated rescue inhaler use with poor relief
Oxygen saturation 90%
Tachycardia and tachypnoea
Intercostal retractions
Speaking in short phrases

questions.rationale: These findings show significant lower airway obstruction and increased work of breathing. A child who cannot speak comfortably and has poor response to home rescue medication may be at risk of severe exacerbation.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Stable allergic rhinitis
Asthma exacerbation with risk of respiratory fatigue and worsening hypoxaemia
Viral rash only
Mild cough only

questions.rationale: This child has more than mild wheeze. The oxygen saturation, work of breathing, and poor response to home medication suggest a potentially severe exacerbation.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Ineffective airway clearance and impaired ventilation related to bronchospasm
Fear of needles only
Disturbed sleep
Need for school absence note

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing come first. Bronchospasm and work of breathing are the primary threats.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Initiate emergency asthma care, support oxygenation, administer or prepare bronchodilator therapy as ordered, and monitor closely
Delay treatment until wheezing stops on its own
Offer a meal before intervention
Encourage the child to lie flat and sleep

questions.rationale: Rapid bronchodilation and oxygen support are key priorities. Delayed treatment can lead to respiratory fatigue and failure.

questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Involve the caregiver and explain what signs show improvement or worsening
Reassess breath sounds, oxygenation, and work of breathing after treatment
Watch for decreasing wheeze with worsening distress, which may indicate less air movement
Prepare for escalation if fatigue increases or oxygenation remains poor
Assume the child is better once medication is given once

questions.rationale: Asthma reassessment is essential. A quieter chest is not always reassuring if airflow is failing. Family support and escalation planning are part of safe paediatric care.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Retractions worsen and oxygen saturation falls further
Monitoring is stopped because the mother feels calmer
The child becomes drowsy and quieter with less audible wheeze
Wheeze lessens but air movement remains good, oxygenation improves, and the child can speak more comfortably

questions.rationale: Improvement must include better airflow and oxygenation, not just less noise. Drowsiness and a quiet chest can mean deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: Which findings support a hypercyanotic spell in tetralogy of Fallot? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knee-drawing behaviour
Known cyanotic congenital heart disease
Irritability
Tachypnoea after crying
Sudden cyanosis

questions.rationale: A hypercyanotic spell often follows crying or stress and includes sudden cyanosis, tachypnoea, irritability, and instinctive flexion or knee-chest positioning. The known cardiac diagnosis is highly relevant.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Mild diaper rash pain only
Simple normal crying episode
Normal feeding discomfort
Hypercyanotic spell causing decreased pulmonary blood flow and reduced oxygenation

questions.rationale: In tetralogy of Fallot, hypercyanotic spells reflect increased right-to-left shunting and reduced oxygenation. The infant requires prompt supportive care.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired oxygenation related to reduced pulmonary blood flow
Disturbed parent sleep
Growth delay only
Delayed tooth eruption

questions.rationale: The immediate danger is poor oxygenation. That must be addressed before education or long-term issues.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay intervention until the father calms down
Place the infant in a knee-chest position, support oxygenation, and reduce agitation while seeking urgent assistance
Lay the infant flat and leave the room
Feed the infant immediately during the spell

questions.rationale: The knee-chest position increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce shunting, improving pulmonary blood flow. Oxygen and calming measures are essential.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor oxygenation and colour trends closely
Ignore these episodes because they always self-resolve safely
Teach the caregiver what to do if another spell occurs
Prepare for escalation if the spell does not improve
Keep stimulation low and comfort the infant

questions.rationale: Caregiver teaching is especially important in congenital cardiac conditions. Spells can be dangerous and should never be dismissed.

questions.sectionLabel: Tetralogy of Fallot with Hypercyanotic Spell
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Cyanosis decreases, breathing eases, oxygenation improves, and the infant settles
Monitoring is stopped because the colour changed slightly
Cyanosis deepens and irritability worsens
The infant becomes limp and less responsive

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better oxygenation, better colour, and reduced distress.

questions.stem: Which findings support Kawasaki disease? Select all that apply.

options.text: Red cracked lips and strawberry tongue
Cervical lymphadenopathy
Swollen erythematous hands and feet
Persistent fever
Conjunctival redness

questions.rationale: All listed findings are characteristic of Kawasaki disease. NCLEX questions often require pattern recognition of prolonged fever plus mucocutaneous inflammation.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Mild food allergy alone
Normal teething symptoms
Simple viral cold only
Kawasaki disease with risk of coronary artery complications

questions.rationale: Kawasaki disease is important because untreated inflammation can affect coronary arteries. Early recognition matters.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for cardiac complications from systemic vasculitis
Disturbed play schedule
Need for school homework planning
Cosmetic skin concern

questions.rationale: The risk of coronary artery involvement makes cardiovascular monitoring and treatment a priority.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Support full assessment, monitor cardiac status, and prepare for IV immunoglobulin and other prescribed therapy
Encourage vigorous physical activity
Send the child home with no follow-up
Delay action because fever in children is common

questions.rationale: The nurse must support treatment promptly because early therapy reduces cardiac complications. Fever should not be dismissed when associated with this pattern.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Educate the caregiver about follow-up for cardiac evaluation
Provide comfort for mucosal discomfort and irritability
Reassess response to therapy
Monitor fever, irritability, hydration, and cardiac status
Ignore extremity changes because they are not important

questions.rationale: Cardiac follow-up is essential. Extremity changes are part of the syndrome and should not be ignored.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: No follow-up is arranged after discharge
Fever decreases, the child becomes less irritable, and cardiac monitoring remains stable as treatment begins
Mucosal findings worsen and monitoring stops
Fever persists and lethargy increases without reassessment

questions.rationale: Improvement includes fever reduction, better comfort, and stable cardiac status.

questions.stem: Which findings support intussusception? Select all that apply.

options.text: Knees drawn to abdomen
Vomiting
Intermittent severe abdominal pain episodes
Lethargy between painful episodes
Red mucousy stool

questions.rationale: This is a classic presentation of intussusception. The alternating pain and lethargy, plus red “currant jelly” stool and vomiting, are important recognition cues.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Possible intussusception with bowel obstruction risk
Mild constipation only
Normal infant colic
Teething distress

questions.rationale: The case suggests telescoping of bowel with intermittent obstruction and vascular compromise. This can become a surgical emergency.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Parent inconvenience
Delayed toy access
Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for bowel ischemia and fluid imbalance

questions.rationale: Bowel compromise and dehydration are the urgent concerns.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Maintain NPO status, support hydration and assessment, and prepare for urgent diagnostic and therapeutic intervention
Delay action because pain comes and goes
Give a large oral feed to calm the child
Send home with only reassurance

questions.rationale: Potential bowel obstruction requires urgent evaluation. Oral feeding could worsen the condition if intervention is needed.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support caregivers with clear explanation
Observe for worsening lethargy or perfusion changes
Prepare for enema reduction or other interventions as ordered
Monitor pain pattern and abdominal status
Assume red stool is harmless dietary colouring

questions.rationale: The stool finding is clinically important and should not be dismissed. Family support is also crucial.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Vomiting worsens and lethargy increases
Pain episodes stop, abdominal distress lessens, and the infant becomes more alert after successful treatment
Abdominal tenderness increases with no escalation
Monitoring stops because the infant is quiet

questions.rationale: Resolution of episodic pain and better responsiveness suggest improved bowel status.

questions.stem: Which findings are concerning for meningitis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe headache
Fever
Photophobia and vomiting
Neck stiffness
Lethargy

questions.rationale: All listed findings are red flags. In paediatrics, meningitis may present with rapid deterioration, so early recognition is critical.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Possible meningitis requiring urgent assessment, infection control, and treatment
Behaviour problem only
Simple tension headache
Mild viral cold only

questions.rationale: The findings indicate a serious central nervous system infection until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Mild stress
Risk for neurological deterioration and sepsis related to meningitis
Delayed mealtime
Disturbed school attendance

questions.rationale: Meningitis can progress rapidly to neurological injury, shock, or death, so urgent management is required.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay action until the child wakes fully
Encourage vigorous play to assess activity tolerance
Support urgent assessment, begin appropriate precautions, and prepare for rapid medical evaluation and treatment
Feed a large meal immediately

questions.rationale: Urgent treatment and appropriate isolation precautions should not be delayed. The child is unstable and potentially infectious.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume drowsiness is harmless because fever is present
Minimise excessive stimulation if the child is photophobic
Watch for seizure activity or worsening responsiveness
Support the caregiver with calm, direct explanations
Monitor neurological status and vital signs closely

questions.rationale: Neurological deterioration, seizures, and worsening responsiveness are important risks in meningitis. Caregiver communication matters in paediatric emergencies.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Seizure-like movements appear with no escalation
Lethargy worsens and perfusion declines
Monitoring is stopped because antibiotics were started
Temperature begins to settle, neurological responsiveness improves, and vital signs become more stable with treatment

questions.rationale: Improvement includes better responsiveness and stabilisation of infection-related instability.

questions.stem: Which features are consistent with a simple febrile seizure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Seizure stopped spontaneously
Age under 5 years
Brief generalised seizure
Sleepy but arousable afterward
Fever at the time of seizure

questions.rationale: These findings fit a simple febrile seizure pattern. Even so, the nurse must assess fully and ensure no additional red flags are present.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Definite chronic epilepsy diagnosis
Likely febrile seizure requiring assessment and supportive management
Normal tantrum behaviour
No further assessment is needed

questions.rationale: A febrile seizure is still a seizure event requiring assessment, but it is often benign when it has the classic pattern described here.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent now?

options.text: Ensuring post-seizure safety and identifying the source of fever
Delayed toy play
Long-term school planning
Need for permanent restraints

questions.rationale: Post-seizure safety and evaluation of the febrile illness are the priorities. Restraints are inappropriate.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Force oral medication immediately while the child is drowsy
Leave the child alone to sleep without monitoring
Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and fever while supporting caregiver reassurance
Delay vital signs until later

questions.rationale: Post-seizure assessment should always include ABCs and responsiveness. Oral intake should be considered only when safe.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Document the seizure history carefully
Evaluate hydration and the cause of fever
Observe for recurrent seizure activity
Provide parent education about what to do if another seizure occurs
Ignore the event because it stopped

questions.rationale: Caregiver education is essential in febrile seizures. The event should not be ignored, even if it stopped before arrival.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates stability?

options.text: No reassessment is performed after the child wakes
The toddler becomes more alert, fever management begins, no further seizure occurs, and ABCs remain stable
Recurrent seizures occur without escalation
The child becomes less responsive and develops breathing difficulty

questions.rationale: Stability after a febrile seizure is shown by recovery of alertness, no recurrent seizure, and stable ABCs.

questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with paediatric DKA? Select all that apply.

options.text: Vomiting and abdominal pain
Dehydration signs
Deep rapid respirations
Polyuria and weight loss history
Fruity breath odour

questions.rationale: All findings strongly support DKA. In children and adolescents, delayed recognition can lead to severe dehydration and cerebral complications.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis with dehydration and metabolic instability
Mild gastroenteritis only
Simple anxiety attack
Stable diabetes control

questions.rationale: This is a classic DKA presentation, not simple gastroenteritis. NGN expects the nurse to link the glucose history, breathing pattern, and dehydration cues.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed body image
Severe metabolic instability with impaired perfusion risk
Missed school concern
Family inconvenience

questions.rationale: The main danger is life-threatening metabolic and fluid imbalance. Perfusion and electrolyte stability must be protected.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage exercise to lower glucose
Offer sugary drinks and delay review
Recognise DKA as an emergency, support monitoring, and prepare for protocol-based fluid and insulin management
Wait until the child asks for treatment

questions.rationale: DKA requires urgent monitored treatment. Fluids, insulin protocols, and close reassessment are essential.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Support the parent and adolescent with brief clear explanation
Trend glucose and electrolytes, especially potassium
Assess urine output and perfusion
Monitor neurological status closely for cerebral oedema risk
Assume improvement once vomiting decreases

questions.rationale: Paediatric DKA requires close neurological observation because children are at risk of cerebral oedema. Electrolyte and perfusion monitoring remain critical.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Hydration improves, glucose trends down appropriately, mental status becomes clearer, and breathing normalises gradually
Vomiting increases and respirations worsen
Drowsiness deepens and perfusion worsens
Monitoring stops after one blood sugar check

questions.rationale: Improvement in DKA is gradual and should include better hydration, glucose control, and neurological status.

questions.stem: Which issues are immediate priorities in a paediatric burn? Select all that apply.

options.text: Burn depth and body surface area estimation
Caregiver distress management
Airway involvement risk if relevant
Prevention of further tissue injury
Pain assessment

questions.rationale: Paediatric burns require a broad safety focus. Pain, severity, airway risk, and further tissue protection are all important. Parents also need guidance so they do not inadvertently worsen the injury.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Burn injury requiring systematic paediatric assessment, pain control, and ongoing monitoring
Rash from allergy only
Minor scratch only
No injury if blistering is present

questions.rationale: This is an acute burn injury requiring structured emergency care and paediatric safety considerations.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for pain, fluid shift, and tissue injury related to burn trauma
Need for homework completion
Mild embarrassment
Delayed playtime

questions.rationale: Pain and tissue injury are immediate concerns, and fluid issues become important depending on burn extent.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Remove stuck clothing by force
Stop the burning process, assess ABCs and burn extent, provide pain support, and protect the wound appropriately
Apply ice directly for prolonged periods
Delay pain management until dressings are chosen

questions.rationale: The nurse must prevent further injury, assess ABCs, and provide pain care. Forceful removal of adherent material and prolonged direct ice can worsen tissue damage.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor for signs of shock if the burn is extensive
Reassess pain using an age-appropriate tool
Provide calm support to the child and parents
Ignore the parent’s questions because treatment is more important
Watch for infection risk as care progresses

questions.rationale: Family support remains part of paediatric care. Pain reassessment and infection prevention are essential.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective early management?

options.text: Perfusion worsens without reassessment
The burn remains exposed and the child becomes more frightened
Monitoring stops after one dressing is placed
Pain becomes more controlled, the wound is protected, ABCs remain stable, and the child appears less distressed

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in better comfort, protected tissue, and stable overall status.

questions.stem: Which findings support failure to thrive? Select all that apply.

options.text: Irritability and low energy
Fewer wet nappies
Poor weight gain trend
Thin extremities
Short ineffective feeds

questions.rationale: Failure to thrive is identified through poor growth plus feeding and hydration concerns. The nurse must recognise both the nutritional and developmental implications.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: No concern if the infant is quiet
Simple teething problem only
Normal infant variation only
Growth failure requiring assessment of intake, health status, and caregiver factors

questions.rationale: Poor growth must be evaluated thoroughly. The causes may be nutritional, medical, developmental, or psychosocial.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Parent inconvenience
Need for toy selection
Inadequate nutrition and hydration affecting growth and development
Sleep pattern only

questions.rationale: The main concern is impaired growth and potentially underlying illness or feeding dysfunction.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore wet nappy pattern
Delay assessment for several months
Assume the infant will outgrow the issue without follow-up
Perform detailed nutritional, hydration, and developmental assessment and collaborate for further evaluation

questions.rationale: A structured assessment is essential in failure to thrive. Delay risks ongoing harm to growth and development.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Watch for medical clues such as vomiting, cardiac strain, or malabsorption signs
Review feeding frequency, duration, and technique
Blame the caregiver without assessment
Examine growth chart trends closely
Assess parent understanding and psychosocial stressors respectfully

questions.rationale: Failure to thrive requires sensitive, nonjudgmental assessment. Causes may be multifactorial and should never be reduced to blame.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement over time?

options.text: Growth continues to fall with no reassessment
Feeding stays poor without follow-up
Parents remain unsupported and confused
Weight gain trend improves, feeding becomes more effective, hydration markers improve, and developmental engagement strengthens

questions.rationale: Improvement is measured through sustained growth, better intake, and improved developmental and hydration status.

questions.stem: Which finding is more suggestive of epiglottitis than croup?

options.text: Hoarse cry
Barking cough
Drooling with muffled voice and tripod positioning
Mild URI symptoms before stridor

questions.rationale: Drooling, muffled voice, high fever, and tripod positioning are classic red flags for epiglottitis and indicate a more dangerous airway emergency than typical croup.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Neither child needs airway concern
Both children can be managed identically
The child with drooling and tripod positioning may have impending airway obstruction and requires higher urgency
Barking cough is always more dangerous than drooling

questions.rationale: The nurse must distinguish between typical croup and epiglottitis-like presentation. Epiglottitis is far more dangerous because agitation or unnecessary examination may worsen obstruction.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent in the child with drooling and tripod positioning?

options.text: Need for food
Risk for sudden airway obstruction
Delayed play
Disturbed sleep

questions.rationale: Potential airway collapse is the life-threatening issue.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first for suspected epiglottitis?

options.text: Force the child to lie flat
Keep the child calm, avoid unnecessary throat examination, and escalate urgently for advanced airway-capable assessment
Delay action until cough develops
Use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat

questions.rationale: Agitation and throat manipulation can worsen obstruction. The nurse should prioritise calm, upright positioning and urgent expert airway support.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume all stridor is low priority
Differentiate croup and epiglottitis using airway severity cues
Reassess stridor, retractions, and energy level frequently
Provide humidified support or ordered therapy for croup while monitoring closely
Involve caregivers in keeping the child calm

questions.rationale: Stridor in children is always important. The nurse must tailor care according to likely cause and severity.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement in the child with croup?

options.text: Drooling begins and is ignored
Stridor decreases, work of breathing lessens, and the child appears calmer after treatment
Monitoring stops when the child becomes quiet without assessment
Retractions worsen and the child becomes more fatigued

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in better airway comfort, less distress, and reduced respiratory effort.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest neurovascular compromise risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Numbness in the fingers
Obvious deformity
Severe pain and swelling
Reduced movement willingness
Coolness distal to the injury

questions.rationale: All findings are important. Numbness and coolness suggest potential compromise of circulation or nerve function. Severe pain with swelling can also signal compartment concerns.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Fracture with possible neurovascular compromise requiring urgent assessment
Behavioural attention-seeking only
Normal playground soreness
Simple bruise only

questions.rationale: The child’s symptoms point beyond pain alone. Distal changes are especially important in extremity injuries.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Parent stress only
Delayed meal
Risk for impaired circulation and nerve function distal to the fracture
Missed school work

questions.rationale: Neurovascular compromise can lead to permanent damage if not identified and managed quickly.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Apply tight wrapping without reassessment
Encourage vigorous finger exercise against resistance immediately
Delay assessment because swelling is expected
Support immobilisation, assess pain and distal circulation/sensation carefully, and prepare for urgent fracture management

questions.rationale: Immobilisation and neurovascular assessment are the priorities. Tight wrapping or delayed reassessment may worsen compromise.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Watch for increasing pain out of proportion to injury
Reassess pulses, colour, warmth, movement, and sensation regularly
Explain procedures clearly to child and caregiver
Provide age-appropriate pain support
Ignore numbness because fractures are painful

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Pain out of proportion and numbness may indicate worsening compartment syndrome or neurovascular injury and must not be ignored.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective early management?

options.text: Monitoring stops after the first splint is applied
Fingers become colder and less responsive
Pain is better controlled, immobilisation is maintained, and distal circulation/sensation remain intact or improve
Numbness worsens without escalation

questions.rationale: Effective management protects the limb, controls pain, and preserves neurovascular function.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: Which findings are concerning for sepsis in this young infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Lethargy and weak response
Temperature instability
Mottled appearance
Poor feeding
Behaviour change from usual pattern

questions.rationale: All these are important warning signs. Neonates and young infants may show infection through poor feeding and subtle behavioural changes rather than dramatic symptoms.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Normal newborn sleepiness only
Minor colic only
Benign fussiness
Possible neonatal/young infant sepsis requiring urgent evaluation

questions.rationale: The infant’s combination of poor feeding, lethargy, and mottling should be treated as high-risk until proven otherwise.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Delayed clothing change
Need for bathing
Risk for overwhelming infection and impaired perfusion
Minor parent inconvenience

questions.rationale: Very young infants can deteriorate rapidly. Perfusion, breathing, and infection management are urgent.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Escalate urgently, assess ABCs and perfusion, support temperature management, and prepare for sepsis evaluation and treatment
Ignore low temperature because fever is absent
Delay action because the infant is quiet
Feed and send home without review

questions.rationale: Absence of high fever does not make sepsis unlikely in very young infants. Quietness and poor feeding are not reassuring.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Communicate clearly with parents while urgent care continues
Reassess temperature and responsiveness frequently
Monitor colour, tone, perfusion, and feeding closely
Assume a sleeping infant is always stable
Prepare for investigations and antimicrobial therapy as ordered

questions.rationale: Ongoing assessment and family communication are essential. A sleeping or quiet infant may actually be unwell and must not be assumed stable.

questions.sectionLabel: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The infant becomes more responsive, feeds better, colour/perfusion improve, and temperature stabilises
Mottling worsens and feeding declines further
Lethargy deepens without escalation
Monitoring is stopped after one observation set

questions.rationale: Improvement in young infants is shown by better responsiveness, feeding, perfusion, and temperature control.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rapid progression after medication exposure
Facial/lip swelling
Throat symptoms
Urticaria
Wheeze and cough

questions.rationale: All findings fit anaphylaxis. The rapid progression after exposure plus airway and skin involvement is especially important.

questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Stable eczema flare
Mild local irritation only
Normal fear response
Systemic allergic reaction with airway compromise risk

questions.rationale: This is not a mild rash. The airway symptoms and rapid progression indicate an emergency.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed play schedule
Risk for airway obstruction and cardiovascular collapse from anaphylaxis
Minor skin irritation only
Need for discharge planning
