questions.rationale: Airway and circulation are the major threats in anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the child to walk around to calm down
Delay action until the rash is measured
Activate emergency response and prepare immediate anaphylaxis treatment according to protocol while supporting airway and oxygenation
Offer food and water

questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis requires immediate treatment. Delay can quickly become life-threatening.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor airway, breathing, circulation, and response to treatment continuously
Reassure the child and caregiver with brief direct explanations
Assume urticaria is the only relevant symptom
Prepare for worsening airway obstruction if treatment is delayed or inadequate
Document the suspected medication allergy clearly

questions.rationale: All listed actions are appropriate except the false assumption that only the skin symptoms matter. Airway risk is central.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The child becomes more cyanotic without escalation
Wheeze decreases, swelling lessens, breathing becomes easier, and the child appears less distressed
Respiratory effort worsens and voice becomes weaker
Monitoring stops because hives improve a little

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in easier breathing and reduction of airway and skin symptoms after emergency treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: Which findings indicate high suicide risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Specific plan to take stored tablets
Social withdrawal and poor intake
Verbalisation of hopelessness
Slow speech and poor eye contact
Statement that others would be better off without her

questions.rationale: All of these cues increase suicide risk. A specific plan with available means is especially high risk. Hopelessness, withdrawal, and self-deprecating statements are classic warning signs. NCLEX mental health questions prioritise direct evidence of intent, plan, and access to means over more general mood symptoms.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: The patient is attention-seeking and should be redirected
The patient has severe depression with active suicidal ideation and requires immediate safety intervention
The patient mainly needs sleep hygiene teaching
The patient is sad but not in immediate danger because she is calm

questions.rationale: A calm tone does not reduce the seriousness of suicidal intent. This patient has depression plus active suicidal ideation, a specific plan, and access to pills. The nurse must interpret the situation as an immediate safety concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Imbalanced nutrition less than body requirements
Social isolation
Risk for self-directed violence related to hopelessness and suicidal plan
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The priority in mental health nursing is always safety. While sleep, nutrition, and isolation are important, the immediate threat to life is self-harm or suicide.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the patient to think positively and join group therapy
Ask the patient to promise not to harm herself and then continue routine rounds
Leave the patient alone for privacy and return later
Stay with the patient, initiate suicide precautions, remove access to harmful objects, and notify the appropriate team immediately

questions.rationale: The first nursing action is to protect the patient. Suicide precautions, direct observation as indicated by policy, environmental safety, and immediate communication are essential. A verbal promise or “no harm contract” is not a replacement for safety measures in a patient with active suicidal intent.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: Which nurse responses are therapeutic and appropriate at this stage? Select all that apply.

options.text: “Can you tell me more about what has been making things feel unbearable?”
“You are being selfish if you try to hurt yourself.”
“We will stay with you and help keep you safe.”
“I’m glad you told me. Your safety is my priority right now.”
“You should not feel this way; think about your family.”

questions.rationale: The therapeutic responses are those that acknowledge the disclosure, invite further expression, and reinforce safety. Judgmental statements and guilt-inducing comments are non-therapeutic and may shut down communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Major Depressive Disorder with Active Suicide Plan
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the immediate nursing plan is effective?

options.text: The patient is told to attend activities without further risk assessment
The patient remains under appropriate observation, harmful items are removed, and she continues to communicate suicidal thoughts openly with staff support
The patient is left alone because she appears quieter
The patient stops talking and the nurse assumes she is improving

questions.rationale: In the first phase of care, effectiveness is shown by maintained safety, environmental control, ongoing assessment, and continued communication. Silence or apparent calm is not enough to prove reduced risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with acute mania? Select all that apply.

options.text: Restlessness and pacing
Grandiose ideas about major success
No sleep for several days
Pressured speech and distractibility
Poor judgment with overspending

questions.rationale: All of these findings are classic features of mania. NCLEX questions often test the nurse’s ability to identify mood elevation, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, impulsivity, and hyperactivity as part of a manic episode.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: Stable bipolar disorder without need for intervention
Acute manic episode with impaired judgment and high risk for exhaustion and unsafe behaviour
Healthy confidence and normal energy
Mild anxiety with caffeine overuse

questions.rationale: This patient is not simply energetic; he is clinically manic. His sleep deprivation, impulsive spending, grandiosity, and lack of insight increase the risk of harm to self and others.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for injury related to impulsivity, poor judgment, and escalating activity
Chronic low self-esteem
Disturbed sleep pattern only
Social isolation

questions.rationale: The most urgent problem is unsafe behaviour caused by impaired judgment and overstimulation. Sleep is important, but the priority is preventing harm and stabilising the environment.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Provide a low-stimulation environment, set clear limits, and assess for immediate safety risks while involving the treatment team
Engage the patient in a long group discussion about business plans
Ignore the behaviour unless he becomes physically aggressive
Challenge the grandiose statements directly and argue with him

questions.rationale: A calm, structured, low-stimulation approach is appropriate. Arguing with grandiose beliefs is non-therapeutic and often escalates the patient. Waiting until aggression occurs misses the opportunity for early intervention.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: Which nursing interventions are appropriate in acute mania? Select all that apply.

options.text: Encourage long emotionally intense group processing sessions
Use short, clear, simple statements
Monitor for exhaustion, dehydration, and medication effects
Offer frequent high-calorie finger foods and fluids as tolerated
Set firm, consistent limits on intrusive behaviour

questions.rationale: Short, direct communication is best when the patient is distractible. Limits help maintain safety. Patients in mania may not sit for meals, so finger foods and hydration are useful. The nurse should also monitor physical depletion and treatment response.

questions.sectionLabel: Bipolar Disorder with Acute Manic Episode
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the plan of care is effective?

options.text: The patient continues pacing continuously without reassessment
The patient shows less agitation, accepts structure, maintains safer behaviour, and begins sleeping for short periods
The nurse stops setting limits to avoid conflict
The patient becomes more overstimulated during group activities and talks faster

questions.rationale: Improvement in acute mania is demonstrated by safer behaviour, reduced stimulation, and the return of some rest or sleep. A lack of structure usually worsens symptoms.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate immediate psychiatric risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Food refusal and withdrawal
Responding to internal stimuli
Command hallucinations telling him to hurt himself
Distractibility during assessment
Guarded, fearful behaviour

questions.rationale: All the findings are significant, but command hallucinations directing self-harm are particularly urgent. Withdrawal and food refusal may worsen physical risk, while fear and distractibility suggest psychotic disorganisation.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient has only mild anxiety
The patient is experiencing psychosis with command hallucinations that may lead to self-harm
The patient simply needs quiet time alone
The patient is pretending to hear voices for attention

questions.rationale: The nurse must take hallucinations seriously, especially when they are command in nature and instruct harm. Dismissing the experience as attention-seeking would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Imbalanced nutrition less than body requirements only
Risk for self-directed violence related to command hallucinations
Social withdrawal
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: Although nutrition and withdrawal matter, self-harm risk is the top priority when the patient is hearing voices telling him to hurt himself.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Immediately challenge the delusion by arguing about reality
Tell the patient the voices are nonsense and to stop talking about them
Leave the patient alone so the hallucinations will pass
Stay with the patient, assess the content and immediacy of the command hallucinations, and initiate appropriate safety precautions

questions.rationale: The correct response is to remain with the patient, explore safety directly, and protect against self-harm. Telling the patient the voices are “nonsense” is invalidating and non-therapeutic. Leaving the patient alone is unsafe.

questions.stem: Which nurse responses are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: “You should just ignore them.”
“When the voices get stronger, please tell staff immediately.”
“I understand the voices are real to you. I do not hear them, but I want to help keep you safe.”
“What are the voices telling you to do right now?”
“The voices are correct about you.”

questions.rationale: These responses validate the patient’s distress without confirming the hallucination as reality. They also assess immediacy and encourage safety communication. Telling the patient simply to ignore the voices is not sufficient in a high-risk situation.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the immediate plan is effective?

options.text: The patient remains safe, stays engaged with staff, reports the voices more openly, and does not act on the command content
The nurse assumes silence means the voices are gone
Food intake is restored but no safety assessment continues
The patient is left isolated because he is quieter

questions.rationale: In the acute phase, effectiveness is measured by safety, engagement, and continued risk assessment—not by superficial quietness.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with a panic attack? Select all that apply.

options.text: Trembling and crying
Tingling in the fingers
Sense of impending doom
Feeling unable to breathe
Hyperventilation

questions.rationale: These are typical panic symptoms. Hyperventilation can lead to dizziness and tingling. Panic symptoms can feel physically overwhelming even when there is no immediate medical life threat.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient is manipulative and should be ignored
The patient has schizophrenia
The patient is calm and simply needs routine teaching
The patient is experiencing an acute panic episode with severe distress and reduced ability to process information

questions.rationale: In a panic state, the person may be unable to take in complex instructions. The nurse should recognise severe anxiety as a real and distressing experience requiring structured support.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about long-term exercise
Social isolation
Disturbed body image
Severe anxiety interfering with breathing pattern and functional coping

questions.rationale: The nurse’s priority is helping the patient regain control of breathing and reduce overwhelming fear enough to re-engage in safe coping.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the patient alone to “get over it”
Confront the patient and say there is nothing wrong
Give lengthy education about cognitive behavioural therapy immediately
Stay with the patient, use short calm statements, reduce stimulation, and coach slow breathing if possible

questions.rationale: The nurse should remain present, speak briefly and calmly, and focus on immediate de-escalation. Panic patients often cannot absorb complex teaching in the acute stage. Dismissive or confrontational responses worsen distress.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: Which responses are therapeutic during acute panic? Select all that apply.

options.text: “Let’s breathe slowly together, one breath at a time.”
“You are safe here. Stay with me and focus on my voice.”
“There is no reason to feel this way.”
“Tell me if the fear is getting stronger or changing.”
“You are overreacting.”

questions.rationale: Therapeutic responses are simple, grounding, and focused on safety and regulation. Telling the patient there is “no reason” or that they are overreacting is non-therapeutic and invalidating.

questions.sectionLabel: Generalised Anxiety with Acute Panic Episode
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The patient stops talking and curls into a ball without follow-up
The nurse leaves before reassessing
Hyperventilation worsens and the patient becomes more disorganised
Breathing becomes slower, the patient can answer more clearly, and visible panic reduces

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduced physiologic arousal and improved ability to communicate and respond.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest a PTSD flashback rather than simple irritability? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sweating and shaking
Hypervigilance and startle response
Disorientation to present surroundings during the episode
Reliving the traumatic event as if it is happening now
External trigger associated with the trauma

questions.rationale: All of these findings are consistent with a trauma-triggered flashback or dissociative episode. The patient is not merely upset—he is temporarily overwhelmed by trauma-related re-experiencing.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Manipulative behaviour to avoid care
Normal post-operative confusion only
Intentional aggression without distress
PTSD flashback with acute fear response requiring grounding and safety support

questions.rationale: The nurse should understand the behaviour through a trauma-informed lens. The patient is frightened and dysregulated, not simply oppositional.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about surgery
Acute fear response with risk of accidental harm to self or others during dissociation
Nutritional imbalance
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The immediate priority is safety during the dissociative or hyperaroused state.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stand over the patient and demand eye contact
Restrain the patient immediately without trying de-escalation
Tell the patient to “snap out of it”
Use a calm voice, create physical and emotional safety, and orient the patient gently to the present

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed care prioritises calm, non-threatening presence, gentle orientation, and reduction of triggers. Immediate restraint without assessing alternatives may worsen trauma.

questions.stem: Which nurse statements are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: “Tell me five things you can see in this room.”
“There is nothing to be afraid of, so stop reacting.”
“Would it help if we reduced the noise and lights?”
“You are in the hospital, and you are safe right now.”
“I’m going to stay with you while you get grounded.”

questions.rationale: Grounding, orientation, and environmental modification are appropriate. Minimising or invalidating the patient’s fear is non-therapeutic.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the immediate plan is effective?

options.text: The patient becomes more oriented to the present, breathing eases, and hypervigilance lessens with support
The patient becomes more agitated and physically defensive
The trigger remains present with no environmental change
The nurse leaves once the patient becomes quiet for a moment

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in reorientation, reduced arousal, and increased sense of safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: Which findings indicate high immediate risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Escalating anger toward staff
Verbal threat to kill herself
Emotional lability and intense fear of abandonment
Threat to self-harm again if left alone
Recent self-harm behaviour

questions.rationale: All of these findings matter. Borderline personality disorder does not reduce the seriousness of suicidal threats or self-harm. The nurse must take all suicidal content seriously while maintaining consistent boundaries.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient mainly wants attention and should be ignored
The patient is manipulative, so the threats are not serious
The patient has no need for assessment because the injuries are superficial
The patient is emotionally dysregulated with real self-harm risk and requires structured, consistent, safety-focused care

questions.rationale: The patient may show manipulative relational patterns, but the nurse must never dismiss self-harm risk. Structured, nonjudgmental care with clear limits is appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Social withdrawal
Risk for self-directed violence related to emotional dysregulation and abandonment fears
Disturbed body image
Knowledge deficit about diet

questions.rationale: The priority is immediate safety. Emotional dysregulation and impulsive self-harm are high-risk features.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Address immediate safety, assess suicidal intent and means, set clear boundaries, and maintain a calm consistent approach
Refuse to speak with her because she is manipulative
Promise the patient special treatment if she stops crying
Debate whether she is truly suicidal

questions.rationale: The nurse should assess risk seriously and provide structured, consistent care. Promising special treatment or withdrawing communication may reinforce maladaptive behaviour or worsen escalation.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: Which responses are therapeutic? Select all that apply.

options.text: “I can see you are very upset. We will deal with one issue at a time.”
“I want to help keep you safe, and we will talk about what happened.”
“You are just trying to manipulate us.”
“We cannot allow self-harm, and we will stay focused on your safety.”
“If you cut again, no one will care.”

questions.rationale: These responses are validating without overinvolvement and set limits without shaming. Judgmental or rejecting statements are inappropriate and may worsen self-harm risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Borderline Personality Disorder with Self-Harm Threat
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Staff respond inconsistently and the patient becomes more volatile
The patient is left alone despite ongoing threats
The patient remains safe, accepts boundaries more consistently, and begins expressing feelings verbally instead of escalating immediately to self-harm threats
The nurse offers special privileges to stop behaviour

questions.rationale: Improvement is measured by safer coping, consistent limit-setting, and reduced reliance on crisis behaviours.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: Which findings indicate severe alcohol withdrawal? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe agitation and insomnia
Tachycardia and hypertension
Tremor and diaphoresis
Visual hallucinations
Recent abrupt cessation of heavy alcohol use

questions.rationale: These are classic signs of escalating alcohol withdrawal. Hallucinations, autonomic instability, and agitation are particularly concerning for severe withdrawal or delirium tremens.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Stable sobriety with no danger
Mild stress only
Schizophrenia onset only
Severe alcohol withdrawal with risk of delirium tremens, seizures, and cardiovascular instability

questions.rationale: This is a high-risk withdrawal pattern. DTs can be life-threatening and require close monitoring and medication management.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Low self-esteem
Social isolation
Disturbed sleep only
Risk for injury, seizure, and autonomic instability related to severe alcohol withdrawal

questions.rationale: Safety and physiological stability are the priorities in severe withdrawal.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Confront the hallucinations by arguing with the patient
Leave the patient alone in a dark room without checks
Delay assessment until the morning
Initiate close withdrawal monitoring, maintain a safe environment, and prepare prescribed withdrawal management promptly

questions.rationale: The patient requires close observation, medication support, and safety measures. Arguing with hallucinations is not helpful, and isolation without monitoring is unsafe.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor vital signs, tremor, orientation, and hallucinations closely
Reduce environmental stimulation while maintaining safety
Encourage hydration and nutrition as tolerated and ordered
Assume hallucinations are harmless if the patient is cooperative
Watch for seizure activity

questions.rationale: Withdrawal may worsen quickly. Hallucinations are not harmless in this context; they signal increasing severity.

questions.sectionLabel: Alcohol Withdrawal with Delirium Tremens Risk
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the plan is effective?

options.text: Tremor and agitation lessen, vital signs stabilise, hallucinations decrease, and the patient remains safe
Seizure precautions are removed early
Monitoring stops because the patient looks tired
Hallucinations worsen and the patient becomes more disoriented

questions.rationale: Improvement in withdrawal is reflected in autonomic stabilisation, less agitation, and fewer perceptual disturbances.

questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with opioid overdose? Select all that apply.

options.text: History of opioid misuse
Pinpoint pupils
Hypoxia and cyanosis
Markedly decreased respiratory rate
Reduced responsiveness

questions.rationale: These are classic features of opioid toxicity. Respiratory depression is the most immediate threat to life.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Panic attack only
Alcohol withdrawal
Likely opioid overdose with life-threatening respiratory depression
The patient is sleeping normally

questions.rationale: The priority is recognising opioid overdose as a respiratory emergency. Reduced responsiveness plus pinpoint pupils and bradypnoea are strongly suggestive.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired ventilation and hypoxia related to opioid overdose
Knowledge deficit about exercise
Social isolation
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: Airway and breathing are always the priority in overdose. Mental health nursing intersects with acute medical safety here.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Support airway and breathing immediately, call for urgent assistance, and prepare for reversal treatment as ordered
Shake the patient and leave if he opens his eyes briefly
Offer oral fluids
Delay intervention until laboratory confirmation

questions.rationale: Immediate respiratory support and emergency response are essential. Waiting for lab confirmation would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous monitoring of respirations, oxygenation, and level of consciousness
Prepare for recurrent sedation after reversal depending on the opioid involved
Maintain patient safety once responsiveness returns
Use calm, direct communication during recovery
Ignore the patient after reversal because the emergency is over

questions.rationale: Opioid overdose management requires ongoing monitoring because respiratory depression may recur. Post-reversal safety and communication are important.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective emergency management?

options.text: The nurse leaves before reassessment
Monitoring is stopped as soon as he wakes up
The patient becomes more cyanotic and unresponsive
Respirations improve, oxygen saturation rises, and the patient becomes more responsive while remaining monitored

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better breathing, better oxygenation, and ongoing observation.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate clinically significant anorexia nervosa? Select all that apply.

options.text: Bradycardia and hypotension
Marked underweight status
Feeling cold and near-fainting
Distorted body image
Excessive exercise and food restriction

questions.rationale: All listed findings are important. The physical signs show medical instability, while body image distortion and extreme control behaviours support the diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Ordinary adolescent insecurity only
Healthy dieting with good self-discipline
Stable nutrition with no risk
Eating disorder with serious medical compromise requiring close monitoring

questions.rationale: The patient has both psychological and physiological danger signs. The nurse must not be reassured by the patient’s denial of illness.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for dysrhythmia, syncope, and further physiological deterioration related to malnutrition
Social withdrawal only
Need for gym access
Disturbed sleep alone

questions.rationale: Medical instability is the immediate priority in severe anorexia, particularly bradycardia, low blood pressure, and risk of collapse.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Begin careful medical and nutritional monitoring, assess immediate physical stability, and support structured treatment with therapeutic communication
Leave all decisions entirely to the patient without monitoring
Argue about calories and force food without assessment
Praise the patient’s self-control

questions.rationale: The nurse must balance medical safety with a calm, nonjudgmental approach. Praise or confrontation can reinforce pathology or escalate resistance.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tell the patient appearance is the only issue
Watch for refeeding-related complications once nutrition improves
Use neutral, nonjudgmental language about food and weight
Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, hydration, and labs closely
Support structured meals as ordered

questions.rationale: Anorexia treatment includes medical monitoring, refeeding safety, and neutral therapeutic communication. The condition is far more serious than appearance concerns.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates early progress?

options.text: Monitoring stops because the patient says she is fine
Staff argue with the patient about appearance
Vital signs become more stable, the patient tolerates structured intake, and engagement with treatment improves gradually
The patient becomes weaker and vital signs worsen

questions.rationale: Early improvement may be gradual, but stabilising physiology and increased engagement are important indicators.

questions.stem: Which findings support serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Agitation and confusion
Recent serotonergic medication change with supplement use
Tremor and hyperreflexia
Sweating and elevated temperature
Diarrhea

questions.rationale: All listed findings are characteristic of serotonin syndrome. This is a high-yield NCLEX medication safety topic in mental health nursing.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Mild anxiety only
Serotonin syndrome requiring urgent medical attention and medication review
Bipolar mania only
Stable antidepressant adjustment

questions.rationale: The combination of autonomic instability, neuromuscular findings, and serotonergic exposure is concerning for serotonin syndrome.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for severe autonomic and neurological instability related to medication interaction
Social anxiety
Mild embarrassment
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: The syndrome can become life-threatening. Immediate physical safety and medication review are priorities.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay action until tomorrow
Tell the patient the symptoms are expected and harmless
Give the next antidepressant dose on time
Hold the suspected serotonergic agents, escalate urgently, and monitor vital signs and neurological status closely

questions.rationale: The nurse must respond urgently, because serotonin syndrome can worsen quickly. Continuing serotonergic medications would be unsafe.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Educate the patient later about avoiding unapproved drug-supplement combinations
Obtain a clear medication and supplement history
Reduce stimulation and maintain safety
Ignore diarrhea because only fever matters
Monitor temperature, heart rate, and rigidity

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. A full medication history is essential because interactions often involve prescription and non-prescription substances.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Monitoring stops after one review
Agitation lessens, temperature and heart rate improve, and neuromuscular findings begin to settle
Medication causes are not clarified
Rigidity worsens and confusion increases

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduced autonomic and neurological instability.

questions.stem: Which findings indicate lithium toxicity? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ataxia and slurred speech
Dehydration after diarrhea
Nausea and vomiting
Elevated lithium level
Coarse tremor

questions.rationale: All these findings support lithium toxicity. Dehydration reduces lithium clearance and can rapidly raise levels.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Simple viral illness only
Lithium toxicity requiring urgent intervention and fluid/renal assessment
Mild expected medication side effect only
Stable mania treatment response

questions.rationale: This is beyond routine mild side effects. Neurological changes plus elevated lithium level signal toxicity.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for worsening neurological toxicity and impaired renal clearance
Mild anxiety
Social isolation
Disturbed sleep only

questions.rationale: The urgent concern is progressive toxicity affecting the nervous system and kidney handling of the drug.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold lithium, assess hydration and neurological status, and notify the provider urgently
Give the next dose with food
Ignore the tremor because lithium always causes shaking
Tell the patient to continue the medication until the next appointment

questions.rationale: The medication should be withheld in suspected toxicity, and the nurse must escalate urgently. Continuing lithium could worsen the condition.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume all tremors on lithium are harmless
Teach the patient later about maintaining hydration and when to seek help
Review recent illnesses, fluid loss, and sodium/fluid intake
Reassess gait, speech, and mental status closely
Monitor fluid balance and renal function

questions.rationale: Lithium safety depends on hydration and kidney function. Patient education about illness, dehydration, and toxicity is crucial.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Ataxia worsens and lithium continues unchanged
The patient becomes more confused without escalation
Monitoring stops after one lab result
Tremor lessens, gait becomes steadier, confusion decreases, and hydration improves after treatment adjustments

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better neurological stability and correction of contributing factors.

questions.stem: Which behaviours indicate increasing risk of violence? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pacing and motor agitation
Clenched fists
Invading personal space
Poor impulse control
Loud, threatening tone

questions.rationale: These are classic escalation cues. Mental health nurses are expected to identify pre-assault behaviour early and intervene before physical violence occurs.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Normal assertiveness only
Escalating aggression with risk of imminent violence if not de-escalated
Harmless frustration only
Positive social interaction

questions.rationale: The cluster of behaviours suggests rising violence risk. Early intervention is safer and less restrictive than waiting until assault occurs.

questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep
Risk for violence directed toward self or others
Low self-esteem
Knowledge deficit about rules

questions.rationale: Safety is the top priority. Potential violence overrides other concerns.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the behaviour until he throws something
Stand very close and argue about the rules
Challenge the patient publicly in front of peers
Use calm de-escalation, maintain safe distance, reduce environmental triggers, and call for support as needed

questions.rationale: The least restrictive effective intervention is calm de-escalation with environmental control and backup if required. Public confrontation or waiting for violence is unsafe.

questions.stem: Which nursing strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offer clear behavioural limits and choices
Mock the patient’s anger to break tension
Keep an exit route available for staff safety
Speak in a calm, low, brief manner
Remove bystanders and reduce stimulation

questions.rationale: These are evidence-based de-escalation principles. Mocking the patient is disrespectful and dangerous.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates successful early de-escalation?

options.text: The environment remains crowded and noisy
The nurse stands trapped in the corner with no support
The patient becomes more physically intimidating and staff continue arguing
The patient’s pacing slows, voice volume decreases, and he responds to simple limit-setting without assaultive behaviour

questions.rationale: Successful de-escalation reduces stimulation, lowers arousal, and prevents injury.

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: Which findings suggest significant depression and self-harm risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Irritability and isolation
Thoughts that others would be better off without her
Withdrawal from friends and school decline
Hopeless statements
Cutting behaviour

questions.rationale: All of these are important risk indicators in adolescent depression. Self-harm, hopelessness, academic decline, and withdrawal are red flags.

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Normal exam stress
Mild attention-seeking only
Adolescent depression with self-harm behaviour and possible suicidal ideation requiring careful safety assessment
Typical teenage mood only

questions.rationale: The pattern goes beyond ordinary adolescent distress. Nurses must not dismiss self-harm or hopelessness as “just a phase.”

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep only
Need for study skills teaching
Risk for self-directed violence related to depression and self-harm
Social media overuse

questions.rationale: Safety is the immediate priority. Depression with self-harm warrants careful suicide assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Focus only on school grades
Tell the mother to handle it alone at home
Avoid asking about suicide because it may give ideas
Conduct a direct but supportive suicide risk assessment and involve appropriate safety planning immediately

questions.rationale: Asking directly about suicide does not create suicidal thoughts; it is necessary for safety. Family involvement may be important, but the nurse must first assess risk clearly.

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: Which therapeutic responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: “When you think people would be better off without you, do you think about killing yourself?”
“We will work on keeping you safe while we understand what’s been happening.”
“This is probably just drama.”
“I’m glad you told me. I want to understand how bad it has been feeling.”
“You have so much to live for, so you should stop cutting.”

questions.rationale: These responses are direct, nonjudgmental, and safety-focused. Minimising or lecturing the adolescent is non-therapeutic.

questions.sectionLabel: Adolescent Depression with Self-Harm and Social Withdrawal
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective immediate care?

options.text: The self-harm history is ignored because wounds are superficial
Suicide risk is clearly assessed, safety planning is initiated, and Maya continues talking honestly with the nurse and team
The nurse avoids further questions after the first answer
Maya is dismissed as dramatic and sent away without assessment

questions.rationale: The key early outcome is honest communication plus structured safety assessment and planning.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: Which findings suggest delirium rather than stable dementia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Visual misperceptions
Pulling at lines and restless behaviour
Sudden onset of confusion
Fluctuating attention and disorientation
Acute worsening from baseline

questions.rationale: Delirium is typically acute, fluctuating, and often associated with medical illness. Visual misperceptions and sudden worsening from baseline are especially important clues.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Stable dementia only
Acute delirium likely related to medical illness, requiring urgent assessment and safety measures
This is simply normal ageing
Personality disorder

questions.rationale: The sudden, fluctuating, perceptual, medically linked change points to delirium. In NCLEX questions, delirium is an urgent reversible medical issue until proven otherwise.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Acute confusion with risk of injury and missed medical deterioration
Social withdrawal
Chronic low self-esteem
Sleep pattern only

questions.rationale: The patient is at risk of injuring herself and may be showing worsening infection or other medical instability.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Argue about the hallucinations and demand orientation
Assume nothing can be done because she is elderly
Reassess medical status, ensure environmental safety, and communicate the acute change promptly to the team
Leave the patient alone in a dark room

questions.rationale: Delirium requires medical reassessment and a safe, calm environment. Arguing about perceptions is not therapeutic.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess for pain, infection, medication effects, and dehydration
Reduce unnecessary stimulation but maintain visibility and supervision
Use restraints as the first intervention
Involve family for reassurance if helpful
Reorient gently and frequently

questions.rationale: Delirium management focuses on treating underlying causes and supporting safety. Restraints are not first-line and should only be considered under strict least-restrictive principles if necessary.

questions.sectionLabel: Delirium versus Dementia in an Older Adult
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Family concerns are ignored
Confusion worsens and no reassessment occurs
Attention and orientation improve, agitation lessens, and the patient becomes more like baseline as the medical issue is treated
The patient is restrained without cause analysis

questions.rationale: Improvement in delirium is shown by clearer attention, safer behaviour, and return toward prior baseline with treatment of the underlying trigger.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which findings are most relevant when considering the medication refusal? Select all that apply.

options.text: He appears calm and oriented
He can state a reason for refusal
He is not currently violent or acutely out of control
He reports side effects from the medication
The patient is voluntary

questions.rationale: All these factors matter. A patient who is calm, oriented, and able to explain refusal may retain the right to refuse medication, depending on jurisdiction and current legal status.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: All psychiatric patients automatically lose the right to refuse medication
The nurse should force the medication immediately
Side effects are irrelevant if the order exists
The patient may have the right to refuse medication, and the nurse must assess capacity, risk, and legal status carefully

questions.rationale: Psychiatric diagnosis alone does not remove patient rights. The nurse must assess capacity, current risk, and legal context rather than assuming forced medication is appropriate.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Sleep pattern documentation only
Balancing patient autonomy and safety through proper assessment of refusal and risk
Teaching about diet first
Group attendance planning

questions.rationale: The nurse must evaluate refusal ethically and legally while ensuring the patient is not at immediate risk to self or others.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the refusal completely
Threaten the patient with punishment
Explore the patient’s concerns, assess understanding and current risk, and follow facility/legal procedures regarding refusal
Hide the medication in food

questions.rationale: The nurse should assess the patient’s understanding, discuss side effects, and follow legal policy. Covert medication and threats violate patient rights and trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Notify the provider if clinically indicated and discuss side effects/alternatives
Assess whether EPS or other adverse effects may be contributing to refusal
Respect the patient’s rights while continuing observation of mental state
Assume refusal means discharge is impossible
Document the refusal objectively and accurately

questions.rationale: These are appropriate ethical and professional responses. The nurse should not jump to punitive conclusions.

questions.sectionLabel: Refusal of Psychiatric Medication and Legal-Ethical Decision-Making
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective and ethical nursing care?

options.text: Medication is forced without legal basis
The patient’s refusal is assessed and documented appropriately, side effects are addressed, and ongoing risk monitoring continues without coercion
The refusal is ignored and no one reassesses mental status
Staff shame the patient into accepting medication

questions.rationale: Effective care respects autonomy while still monitoring safety and engaging the patient in treatment decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: Which findings suggest a possible problem with informed consent? Select all that apply.

options.text: The form is signed in the chart
Staff pressure exists to keep the schedule moving
The patient appears anxious and uncertain
He has unanswered questions about the surgical outcome
The patient says he does not understand the procedure fully

questions.rationale: The important cues are not the signature but the patient’s current lack of understanding and unresolved questions. Time pressure from staff can create unsafe shortcuts. Anxiety may occur in any pre-op patient, but when combined with confusion and unanswered questions, it signals a consent concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The nurse should explain the surgery in full and obtain a new consent independently
The patient is simply nervous and should be reassured without delay
Consent is complete because the form is signed
The patient may not have provided truly informed consent and further clarification is needed before proceeding

questions.rationale: Informed consent requires understanding, voluntariness, and capacity. A signed document is not enough if the patient still does not understand. The nurse can witness and verify the process, but the procedural explanation and consent responsibility belong to the provider performing the procedure.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Maintaining the operating room schedule
Reducing pre-operative paperwork burden
Protecting the patient’s right to informed decision-making before surgery proceeds
Avoiding conflict with the surgical team

questions.rationale: Patient autonomy and legal consent take priority over efficiency or staff convenience. Proceeding without true informed understanding risks ethical and legal harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ask the family to explain the surgery and proceed
Send the patient to theatre and let the anaesthetist answer questions later
Pause the pre-operative progression, notify the surgeon or responsible provider, and ensure the patient’s questions are addressed before transfer
Tell the patient it is too late to ask questions because the form is signed

questions.rationale: The nurse should stop the process long enough to ensure valid consent. Family explanation is not a substitute for the responsible provider’s explanation. Proceeding without clarification would be unsafe and unethical.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess whether the patient is currently oriented and able to participate in decision-making
Advocate for the patient even if staff are frustrated by delay
Avoid discussing the issue to prevent conflict with the surgeon
Use calm, respectful communication to support the patient’s questions
Document the patient’s statements and the actions taken objectively

questions.rationale: All these are appropriate. Nurses have a duty to advocate, document clearly, and assess the patient’s present ability to participate. Avoiding the issue to prevent conflict would neglect professional responsibility.

questions.sectionLabel: Informed Consent and Patient Confusion Before Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing management?

options.text: Family pressure replaces provider explanation
The patient receives clarification from the appropriate provider, demonstrates better understanding, and surgery proceeds only after valid consent is confirmed
Staff avoid documentation because the schedule was delayed
The patient remains confused but is transferred because the form is signed

questions.rationale: Effective management protects autonomy, ensures legal-ethical compliance, and still allows care to proceed safely once true informed consent is present.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: Which findings are most relevant when evaluating this refusal? Select all that apply.

options.text: She can state the reason for refusal
The patient is alert and oriented
The medication is routinely prescribed
She understands the purpose and consequences
Another nurse suggests covert administration

questions.rationale: All these details matter. The patient appears to have decision-making capacity regarding this medication, and covert administration would violate rights and trust. The fact that the medication is routinely prescribed does not cancel the patient’s right to refuse.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Refusal means the patient loses all other rights to participate in care
A competent patient may refuse treatment, and the nurse must assess, educate, document, and notify as appropriate
Prescribed medications must always be given regardless of refusal
Crushing medication secretly is acceptable if the nurse believes it is beneficial

questions.rationale: Respect for autonomy means competent adults may refuse medication after understanding the implications. The nurse should assess the reason, provide education, document accurately, and communicate appropriately.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Respecting autonomy while ensuring the patient understands the risks and alternatives
Preventing any future discussion of side effects
Avoiding inconvenience for the medication round
Teaching the patient about unrelated discharge topics

questions.rationale: The nurse’s immediate priority is ethical decision-making that respects the patient’s rights while ensuring informed refusal.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hide the medication in juice so the patient still receives it
Tell the patient refusal is not allowed in hospital
Explore the patient’s concerns, clarify the risks and benefits, and document the refusal accurately while notifying the provider if needed
Walk away without documenting the event

questions.rationale: The correct response is respectful exploration, education, documentation, and communication. Covert medication is unethical and may be illegal.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess whether timing adjustments or symptom management could help address the patient’s concerns
Document the refusal factually without judgmental language
Respect the patient’s decision while continuing to monitor clinical status
Communicate the refusal to the provider if clinically indicated
Shame the patient by warning that she is being difficult

questions.rationale: These actions support ethical nursing practice. The nurse can advocate for practical solutions while still respecting the patient’s right to decline.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Refusal by a Competent Adult
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing care?

options.text: The medication is administered secretly to avoid charting a refusal
No one documents the refusal because the patient is familiar with the medication
Staff pressure the patient until she takes it out of fear
The patient’s refusal is respected and documented, her concerns are addressed honestly, and her clinical status is monitored appropriately

questions.rationale: Safe, professional nursing care respects autonomy, documents clearly, and maintains patient safety through ongoing assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: Which facts are most important when deciding what to delegate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Need for ongoing RN evaluation
The complexity of the task
Patient stability
Scope of the UAP role
Whether assessment or teaching is required

questions.rationale: All of these are essential delegation considerations. NCLEX frequently tests delegation using the principles of right task, circumstance, person, direction, and supervision.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Routine, predictable tasks for stable patients may be delegated, but assessment, teaching, and unstable situations remain RN responsibilities
Any task may be delegated if the nurse is busy enough
Discharge teaching may always be given by UAPs
Newly post-operative instability is appropriate for UAP monitoring alone

questions.rationale: Delegation is based on stability and task complexity. RN-only functions include assessment, teaching, clinical judgment, and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: Which delegation decision is safest?

options.text: Ask the UAP to complete anticoagulant discharge teaching
Ask the UAP to independently interpret abnormal vital signs
Ask the UAP to assist the stable dialysis patient with lunch setup and provide the routine bed bath for the stable patient
Ask the UAP to assess the unstable post-operative patient’s deterioration

questions.rationale: Routine tasks for stable patients are appropriate to delegate. Teaching, interpretation, and care of unstable patients are not.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Match the task to the appropriate person and provide clear direction and follow-up expectations for delegated care
Let the UAP decide which patients are stable enough
Delegate everything and sort it out later
Avoid delegation entirely even for routine tasks

questions.rationale: Safe delegation requires clear assignment, expected observations to report, and RN oversight. The RN remains accountable for the delegation decision.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate when delegating? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoid delegating patient education that requires judgment
Reassess the patient personally if the UAP reports a concerning change
Evaluate whether the delegated task was completed safely
Assume no supervision is needed once the task is assigned
Give specific instructions about what findings must be reported immediately

questions.rationale: Delegation includes supervision and evaluation. The RN does not abandon accountability after handing off a task.

questions.sectionLabel: Delegation to an Unlicensed Assistive Personnel
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective delegation?

options.text: The UAP teaches anticoagulant side effects and the RN never checks understanding
The unstable patient deteriorates while delegated assessment is delayed
The RN cannot explain why the task was delegated
Stable routine care is completed appropriately, concerning findings are reported back promptly, and RN-only tasks remain with the nurse

questions.rationale: Effective delegation improves care efficiency without compromising scope, safety, or professional responsibility.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: Which findings confirm that a medication error has occurred? Select all that apply.

options.text: Another staff member suggests not reporting
The nurse recognised the error after administration
The order clearly specified a lower dose
The wrong dose was administered
The patient is not yet symptomatic

questions.rationale: A medication error occurred the moment the wrong dose was administered. The absence of symptoms does not remove the error or the need to act. Staff pressure to hide the error is a serious professionalism concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: If no harm is visible, reporting is unnecessary
The error requires immediate assessment, provider notification, documentation, and reporting according to policy
The nurse should rewrite the MAR to match what was given
The safest action is to wait and see

questions.rationale: Professional integrity and patient safety require prompt action. Delaying response can worsen harm if adverse effects develop.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Preventing unit gossip
Avoiding extra paperwork
Protecting the nurse from embarrassment
Protecting the patient from adverse effects related to the wrong dose

questions.rationale: The patient’s safety is always the priority after an error. The nurse’s emotional discomfort is secondary.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hide the medication packaging and say nothing
Wait for symptoms before intervening
Ask the next shift to handle it
Assess the patient immediately, monitor for adverse effects, and notify the provider while preparing appropriate follow-up

questions.rationale: The correct response begins with patient assessment and communication. Hiding the error is unethical and unsafe.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Complete an incident report according to policy
Document factually what occurred and the patient’s response
Communicate honestly within the appropriate reporting process
Participate in review of factors that contributed to the error
Change the chart to reflect the dose that should have been given

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate professional responses. Altering the record would be falsification and a serious legal-ethical violation.

questions.sectionLabel: Medication Error and Professional Reporting Duty
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective professional management?

options.text: The nurse avoids reporting because the patient had no symptoms
The patient is monitored and protected, the event is reported honestly, and contributing system issues are addressed for prevention
The chart is altered to avoid investigation
The error becomes unit gossip instead of formal reporting

questions.rationale: Ethical nursing practice supports patient safety, truth-telling, and system improvement after errors.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: Which elements make this a confidentiality breach? Select all that apply.

options.text: Discussion occurred in a public elevator
The conversation included family details
A third party recognized the patient
The patient’s name and diagnosis were spoken aloud
Sensitive health information was shared outside a private clinical context

questions.rationale: All of these contribute to a clear confidentiality breach. Protected health information should not be discussed in public areas where unauthorized people may hear.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Public discussion is fine if the patient is not in the elevator
A serious privacy and confidentiality breach has occurred and requires corrective action
This is acceptable because both speakers were nurses
The problem exists only if it appears on social media

questions.rationale: The location and the identifiability of the patient make this a clear breach. Privacy rules apply regardless of whether the patient is physically present.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Moving the conversation to another elevator
Protecting patient privacy and addressing professional misconduct promptly
Keeping the event informal to save time
Avoiding awkwardness among staff

questions.rationale: The immediate priority is to address the breach, protect the patient, and prevent recurrence.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: What should the charge nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the inappropriate discussion, address the breach promptly, and follow facility reporting or managerial procedures as required
Continue the conversation in a quieter public hallway
Ask the visitor not to mention it again and do nothing else
Ignore it because the information was already said

questions.rationale: The breach must be addressed immediately and professionally. Allowing it to continue would worsen the violation.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume confidentiality only applies to electronic records
Document or report the breach according to policy if required
Limit access to information to those directly involved in care
Reinforce that patient information should be discussed only in appropriate private clinical settings
Use the incident as a professional teaching moment on confidentiality

questions.rationale: These are all appropriate. Confidentiality applies in verbal, written, and electronic communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Breach of Confidentiality in a Public Area
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The inappropriate discussion stops immediately, the breach is addressed through proper channels, and staff privacy awareness improves
Patient information is shared casually in hallways afterward
Staff continue discussing patients in public because it is convenient
The event is dismissed because no chart was accessed

questions.rationale: Effective management protects privacy and strengthens professional behaviour going forward.

questions.stem: Which features make this post unsafe or unprofessional? Select all that apply.

options.text: The student used a personal account
The caption references a tragic clinical situation
Social media posts can breach privacy even without a patient name
It was taken in a clinical environment
Potentially identifying details are visible in the background

questions.rationale: All of these are relevant. Personal accounts do not remove professional obligations, and de-identification may fail if contextual details remain visible.

questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The post is harmless because no full name is shown
The post may violate confidentiality and professional standards and must be addressed promptly
Only direct patient selfies are prohibited
Students are exempt from social media rules

questions.rationale: Clinical content on personal social media can breach privacy and damage professionalism even when names are omitted.

questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Preventing further privacy breach and addressing the professional violation immediately
Protecting the student from embarrassment only
Avoiding all discussion of the event
Waiting to see whether the post gets more likes

questions.rationale: The priority is limiting harm and addressing the breach through appropriate supervisory channels.

questions.stem: What should the supervising nurse do first?

options.text: Share the post privately with friends as a warning example
Comment publicly under the post to criticize the student
Ignore the post because it is outside work hours
Instruct the student to remove the post immediately and escalate the matter according to policy

questions.rationale: The content should be removed immediately, and the issue should be handled professionally through policy-based processes.

questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assume the issue ends once the post is deleted
Use the event as education on professional boundaries and digital conduct
Document/report the incident if required by policy
Reinforce that even indirect identifiers can breach confidentiality
Review facility policy on privacy and social media use

questions.rationale: Deleting the post helps, but the incident may still require reporting and education. Professional standards extend to online conduct.

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: The post is removed promptly, the incident is handled according to policy, and the student demonstrates improved understanding of digital professionalism
Staff mock the student instead of educating and reporting appropriately
The post remains online because no full name is visible
Similar posts continue because no one addressed the issue

questions.rationale: Effective management reduces ongoing harm and supports professional learning and accountability.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: Which findings suggest a potential boundary problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Request for personal phone number
Extra time spent in a nonclinical personal role
Increasing personal disclosure by the nurse
Expensive gifts from the patient
Patient’s limited family support

questions.rationale: All of these are relevant. Patient vulnerability does not justify crossing boundaries. Gifts, personal contact, and self-disclosure may shift the relationship away from therapeutic purpose.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: Gifts prove the care is effective and should be accepted
Personal friendships with patients are encouraged if intentions are good
The relationship may be moving beyond therapeutic boundaries and requires corrective action
This is harmless kindness and should continue

questions.rationale: Professional boundaries exist to protect patients and preserve safe care. Good intentions do not remove risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Delaying discharge planning
Maintaining therapeutic boundaries to prevent exploitation or impaired judgment
Preserving gift-giving etiquette
Avoiding discomfort in saying no

questions.rationale: The priority is protecting the patient and ensuring the nurse’s clinical judgment remains professional and unbiased.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Continue self-disclosure to build trust
Re-establish professional boundaries, decline inappropriate gifts or personal contact, and seek supervisory guidance if needed
Accept the gifts but avoid mentioning them
Give the patient a private number to ease loneliness

questions.rationale: The nurse should re-establish boundaries immediately. Accepting gifts or personal contact risks exploitation and professional misconduct.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reflect on countertransference or personal emotional involvement
Document relevant boundary issues if required by policy or the care situation
Use therapeutic communication while keeping the relationship professionally focused
Involve the team if boundary concerns may affect care
Assume that because the patient requested it, the contact is ethically acceptable

questions.rationale: These actions support safe, ethical practice. Patient request alone does not make a boundary crossing acceptable.

questions.sectionLabel: Professional Boundary Crossing with a Patient
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Clinical judgment becomes influenced by favoritism
The nurse accepts gifts and continues private communication after discharge
Staff ignore the issue because the patient is lonely
The nurse maintains a professional therapeutic relationship, declines inappropriate contact, and care remains patient-centred and ethically sound

questions.rationale: Effective management restores and preserves therapeutic boundaries while still offering compassionate care.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: Which findings raise concern for possible elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.

options.text: Controlling family member behaviour
Unexplained healing burn
Dehydration
Patient fearfulness and reluctance to speak
Bruises of different ages

questions.rationale: All of these are classic abuse or neglect warning signs. The patient’s fear and the controlling behaviour of the relative are especially concerning.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The patient may be experiencing abuse or neglect and requires protection and reporting according to law/policy
Family privacy should always override nursing concern
The injuries are normal for ageing and should not be questioned
Reporting is unnecessary unless the patient signs a written complaint

questions.rationale: The nurse must not dismiss suspicious patterns. Mandatory reporting laws and safeguarding responsibilities may apply even if the patient is frightened or reluctant.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Completing discharge paperwork first
Avoiding conflict with the family member
Protecting the patient from further harm while initiating appropriate assessment and reporting steps
Preserving family reputation

questions.rationale: Patient safety and protection are the priority. The nurse must act on suspicious findings rather than avoid discomfort.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Ignore the injuries because the patient asked not to make trouble
Ensure the patient is assessed privately and safely, document objective findings, and follow mandatory reporting or safeguarding procedures promptly
Confront the nephew aggressively in the hallway
Promise absolute secrecy and do nothing

questions.rationale: The nurse should focus on safe assessment, objective documentation, and formal reporting pathways. Confrontation without a plan may increase danger.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Decide alone that no report is needed because the patient seems embarrassed
Document findings objectively, including statements made by the patient
Maintain awareness that fear may limit disclosure
Involve social work, safeguarding, or the appropriate protective services as required
Avoid leading questions during assessment

questions.rationale: These are appropriate actions. Abuse assessments require careful documentation, interdisciplinary support, and avoidance of assumptions or leading language.

questions.sectionLabel: Suspected Elder Abuse and Mandatory Reporting
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective nursing management?

options.text: Documentation is vague and incomplete
Staff ignore the pattern of injuries to avoid conflict
The family is allowed to take the patient home immediately without review
The patient is protected, objective findings are documented, and the concern is reported through the proper safeguarding process

questions.rationale: Effective management protects the vulnerable patient and follows legal-professional obligations.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: Which findings indicate that the order is unsafe? Select all that apply.

options.text: The allergy is visible on the chart and wristband
Another staff member suggests giving it anyway
The patient is septic and treatment is urgent
A documented severe allergy exists
The ordered medication matches the allergy

questions.rationale: All these details matter. Urgency increases complexity, but it does not justify ignoring a known severe allergy. Staff pressure can contribute to unsafe decisions.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s best interpretation?

options.text: The nurse has no role in questioning orders
The antibiotic should be given because speed matters more than allergy history
The order is unsafe and must be questioned immediately; the nurse must advocate for an alternative
Wristband allergies are only advisory, not clinically important

questions.rationale: Professional nursing requires active safety advocacy. A nurse must not knowingly administer a drug that may cause severe harm when a documented allergy exists.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: Which issue is most urgent?

options.text: Finishing the medication round on time
Keeping the workflow simple
Preventing serious medication-related harm from an unsafe order
Avoiding disagreement with the provider

questions.rationale: The patient’s immediate safety is the priority, even under time pressure.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Hold the medication, clarify the allergy/order conflict urgently, and escalate through the appropriate chain if the provider is unavailable
Delete the order independently without communication
Administer the antibiotic and document the allergy later
Ignore the wristband because the infection is severe

questions.rationale: The nurse should not administer the unsafe medication. Urgent escalation and clarification are necessary to protect the patient.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Escalate to a supervisor or rapid chain-of-command process if necessary
Document the clarification process and patient allergy clearly
Assume provider authority overrides all nursing safety concerns
Review whether an alternative appropriate antibiotic has been ordered or can be requested promptly
Use assertive professional communication to explain the safety concern

questions.rationale: These are all correct advocacy actions. Professional accountability includes speaking up when an order is unsafe.

questions.sectionLabel: Unsafe Provider Order and Nursing Advocacy
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective advocacy?

options.text: The nurse gives the medication despite the known allergy
The unsafe medication is not given, the allergy conflict is addressed promptly, and a safer treatment plan is implemented
The allergy remains undocumented in follow-up communication
Staff delay action because they do not want conflict

questions.rationale: Effective advocacy prevents harm, even in urgent situations.

questions.stem: Which findings are most important in this end-of-life conflict? Select all that apply.

options.text: The patient is now unable to speak for himself
